    "description": "We begin the episode with the absolutely ingenious and surprising way in which Kepler discovered the laws of planetary motion.\n\nPeople sometimes say that AI will make especially fast progress at scientific discovery because of tight verification loops. But the story of how we discovered the shape of our solar system shows how the verification loop for correct ideas can be decades (or even millennia) long.\n\nDuring this time, what we know today as the better theory can often actually make worse predictions (Copernicus's model of circular orbits around the sun was actually less accurate than Ptolemy's geocentric model). And the reasons it survives this epistemic hell is some mixture of judgment and heuristics that we don’t even understand well enough to actually articulate, much less codify into an RL loop.\n\nHope you enjoy!\n\n𝐄𝐏𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐃𝐄 𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐊𝐒\n* Transcript: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/terence-tao\n* Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/terence-tao-kepler-newton-and-the-true/id1516093381?i=1000756353875\n* Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/episode/24xF8YGra2w3HXZYbhgVKU?si=U5V-SgvSQ8eVIcG2Z86wfQ\n\n𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐍𝐒𝐎𝐑𝐒\n- Jane Street loves challenging my audience with different creative puzzles. One of my listeners, Shawn, solved Jane Street’s ResNet challenge and posted a great walk-through on X ( https://x.com/hynwprk/status/2026376546286711206 ). If you want to try one of these puzzles yourself, there’s one live now at https://janestreet.com/dwarkesh\n- Labelbox can get you rubric-based evals, no matter your domain. These rubrics allow you to give your model feedback on all the dimensions you care about, so you can train how it thinks, not just what it thinks. Whatever you’re focused on—math, physics, finance, psychology or something else—Labelbox can help. Learn more at https://labelbox.com/dwarkesh\n- Mercury just released a new feature called Insights. Insights summarizes your money in and out, showing you your biggest transactions and calling out anything worth paying attention to. It’s a super low-friction way to stay on top of your business. Learn more at https://mercury.com/insights\n\nTo sponsor a future episode, visit https://dwarkesh.com/advertise.\n\n𝐓𝐈𝐌𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐀𝐌𝐏𝐒\n00:00:00 – Kepler was a high temperature LLM\n00:11:44 – How would we know if there’s a new unifying concept within heaps of AI slop?\n00:26:10 – The deductive overhang\n00:30:31 – Selection bias in reported AI discoveries\n00:46:43 – AI makes papers richer and broader, but not deeper\n00:53:00 – If AI solves a problem, can humans get understanding out of it?\n00:59:20 – We need a semi-formal language for the way that scientists actually talk to each other\n01:09:48 – How Terry uses his time\n01:17:05 – Human-AI hybrids will dominate math for a lot longer",

      "id": "UgxNx7DGQcpIHwpg_rB4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "---\r\n\r\n## Key Points\r\n\r\n- *Kepler’s Approach as Early Data Science:* Trial-and-error hypothesis testing grounded in Tycho Brahe’s precise observational data led to the first accurate model of planetary orbits (ellipses vs. circles) (00:00–00:04:22).  \r\n- *AI’s Role is Shifting Science Bottlenecks:* AI excels at generating vast numbers of hypotheses; the new bottleneck is systematic validation and assessment of scientific ideas at scale (00:04:22–00:13:21).  \r\n- *Scientific Progress Involves Culture and Narrative:* Beyond raw data and theories, social acceptance, communication, and storytelling drive the adoption of new scientific ideas (00:13:22–00:18:45).  \r\n- *Serendipity and Unstructured Exploration Are Crucial:* Accidental discoveries and random interactions foster creative leaps that highly optimized workflows risk losing (00:18:45–00:26:52, 01:07:53–01:16:06).  \r\n- *AI Triumphs in Breadth, Humans in Depth:* AI can quickly solve many simpler problems or identify partial paths, but humans provide deep insight, creativity, and interpretability (00:26:52–00:36:54).  \r\n- *Mathematical Research Values Process, Not Just Results:* The journey of discovery cultivates intuition and expertise; immediate answers from AI might risk hampering deep understanding (00:36:54–00:43:42).  \r\n- *Current AI Mostly Applies Known Techniques:* AI workflows often replicate and recombine existing methods better than humans but rarely create new theories (00:43:42–00:49:06).  \r\n- *Intelligence vs. Cleverness:* True intelligence requires cumulative learning and adapting strategies interactively, something current AIs cannot yet replicate (00:49:06–00:56:59).  \r\n- *Formal Languages and Proof Assistants Enable Precise Analysis:* Tools like Lean can decompose proofs into atomic units, facilitating AI collaboration in proof refinement and understanding (00:57:00–01:02:27).  \r\n- *Measuring Scientific Progress is Complex:* Progress depends on historical context, validation over time, and often retrospective acceptance, complicating how AI might assess scientific merit (01:02:27–01:07:53).  \r\n- *AI Will Reshape Scientific Workflows:* Future science will rely on broad AI-generated hypotheses and human expert interpretation, requiring new scientific and publication paradigms (01:16:06–01:23:11).  \r\n- *Advice for Aspiring Mathematicians:* Stay adaptable, leverage AI tools early, embrace new ways of doing science, and cultivate openness to both traditional and emerging methods (01:23:11–End).  \r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## Key Insights\r\n\r\n- 🪐 *Analogy of Kepler as an Early “high-temperature LLM”* (00:04:00): Kepler’s process of trying random geometric hypotheses resembles how large language models explore solution spaces—intuitive but needing validation.  \r\n- 🧩 *Bottleneck Shift from Idea Generation to Validation* (00:12:00): AI exponentially lowers the cost of generating hypotheses, creating urgent demand for scalable validation frameworks, peer review, and filtering mechanisms.  \r\n- 📊 *AI and Data-First Hypothesis Generation* (00:08:00): Unlike traditional model-first science, modern science is increasingly data-driven—observations precede hypotheses. AI can amplify this data-first method.  \r\n- 🌄 *Mountain Climbing Metaphor for AI in Math* (00:32:00): AI can summit smaller, more accessible “walls” (problems) in math but struggles with deeper challenges due to lack of partial progress evaluation.  \r\n- 🚀 *Complementarity of AI Breadth and Human Depth* (00:35:00): Human experts have unparalleled depth in complex reasoning, while AI offers unparalleled breadth, enabling new modes of collaborative science.  \r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)\r\n\r\n*Q1: Can AI independently solve major unsolved math problems like the Riemann hypothesis?*  \r\n*A:* Likely not fully autonomously. Such problems probably require new conceptual math beyond brute force and will involve deep human-AI collaboration and insight (00:53:00–00:56:59).\r\n\r\n*Q2: How do we distinguish between useful AI-generated scientific ideas and noise?*  \r\n*A:* Current methods are overwhelmed. New validation, peer review, and possibly automated scientific frameworks are needed to filter progress reliably (00:12:00–00:14:00).\r\n\r\n*Q3: Does AI improve mathematical productivity or mainly routine tasks?*  \r\n*A:* AI currently accelerates auxiliary and routine tasks, enriching outputs, but the core deep creative processes still rely on human insight for now (00:47:00–00:49:30).\r\n\r\n*Q4: How important is serendipity in science and math discovery?*  \r\n*A:* Crucial—random encounters and inefficient exploration foster unexpected insights that systematic optimization often misses (01:07:53–01:16:06).\r\n\r\n*Q5: How can early-career mathematicians prepare for an AI-influenced research landscape?*  \r\n*A:* Be adaptable, embrace AI tools, pursue both traditional credentials and innovative methods, and remain curious and open to different problem-solving approaches (01:21:00–End).\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## Conclusion\r\n\r\nThe conversation with Terence Tao underscores that the nature of scientific progress is evolving alongside AI—not by replacing human creativity but by augmenting it, particularly by massively lowering the cost of exploration and hypothesis generation. Historical breakthroughs were forged through painstaking data collection paired with inspired hypothesis testing, a process AI now accelerates at unprecedented scales. Yet, the critical bottleneck remains rigorous validation, discernment, and the artful human narrative that cements scientific ideas into lasting knowledge. Future scientific success hinges on rethinking workflows to harness AI’s breadth with human depth, fostering new hybrid collaboration modes, and preserving the randomness and serendipity essential for innovation.\r\n\r\n*Action Suggestions:*  \r\n- Develop scalable validation systems for handling AI-generated scientific outputs.  \r\n- Foster interdisciplinary collaboration combining AI expertise with deep human insight.  \r\n- Encourage early-career researchers to adopt flexible learning strategies incorporating AI tools.  \r\n- Promote new scientific communication paradigms that blend formal rigor with accessible narratives.  \r\n- Support research into semi-formal frameworks capturing scientific reasoning beyond formal proofs.\r\n\r\nThe video invites viewers to embrace the uncertain yet thrilling transformation of science by AI, where tradition meets innovation to redefine discovery’s future.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCXURLs8PLUwlx5yeTWg1Fcg",
      "author": "@AnthonyOlszewskiJerseyCity",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mIhvVWJC2kBKrZH3noKAK-wh4-jB5ZGhcTpLUkGH5XPGE=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,

      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyNeW_SoZyq9c9Yq6F4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "## Summary\r\n\r\nThis video presents an extensive and insightful conversation with Terence Tao, a preeminent mathematician, exploring the evolving landscape of scientific discovery, especially the role of AI in mathematics and research. The central theme is how historical scientific breakthroughs, like Kepler’s laws of planetary motion, emerged from a blend of hypothesis, data, and iteration—and how AI might transform this process today and in the future. The discussion emphasizes the complementary relationship between human creativity and AI’s brute force capabilities, the challenges in scientific validation with AI-generated ideas, and the importance of evolving scientific methods to harness AI’s strengths.\r\n\r\n*Who is it suitable for:*  \r\n- Mathematicians, scientists, and researchers interested in AI’s impact on scientific discovery.  \r\n- Students and professionals curious about the history and philosophy of science.  \r\n- AI enthusiasts wanting to understand the challenges and opportunities in integrating AI with math research.  \r\n\r\n*What readers can learn:*  \r\n- The history of scientific discovery framed through Kepler and Newton’s contributions.  \r\n- A detailed analysis of AI’s role in hypothesis generation versus validation in science.  \r\n- Insights into how mathematics and science workflows might shift with AI augmentation.  \r\n- The differences between clever problem-solving and genuine scientific intelligence.  \r\n- Practical advice for early-career mathematicians and scientists navigating an AI-augmented landscape.  \r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## Timeline Summary\r\n\r\n*00:00–00:04:22 | Kepler’s Discovery and Early Scientific Data*  \r\nTerence recounts Kepler’s path from Copernicus’s heliocentric model to his Platonic solids theory and how Tycho Brahe’s precise data enabled the breakthrough discovery that planetary orbits are elliptical, laying the foundations of modern astronomy.\r\n\r\nConclusion: Early science balanced elegant hypothesis generation with meticulous data collection, highlighting the necessity of both.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*00:04:22–00:07:38 | AI as a Modern Analogy to Historical Science*  \r\nDiscussion about how Kepler’s trial-and-error method resembles modern AI’s random hypothesis generation, but with the essential twist that validation against high-quality data is crucial. The bottleneck has shifted from idea generation to systematic verification.\r\n\r\nConclusion: AI can generate ideas at scale, but scientific progress relies heavily on verifying and vetting these ideas.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*00:07:38–00:13:21 | The Changing Paradigm of Scientific Discovery*  \r\nScience has evolved from theory-experiment to simulation and now big data-driven hypothesis generation. The increase in AI-generated scientific output creates an urgent need to redesign peer review and validation systems to handle the flood of ideas.\r\n\r\nConclusion: The scalability of idea generation demands new, scalable ways to evaluate scientific merit.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*00:13:22–00:18:45 | Long-Term Validation and Scientific Culture*  \r\nExamples from history show that new theories often face initial resistance or are less accurate than existing ones yet provide deeper understanding long-term. The social narrative and communication of science play a critical role in acceptance and progress.\r\n\r\nConclusion: Scientific progress is iterative, sometimes contentious, and dependent on culture and communication.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*00:18:45–00:26:52 | Serendipity, Insight, and the Deductive Overhang in Science*  \r\nTao highlights the importance of serendipity, narrative-building, and deep insight in science, with examples from Darwin’s clear exposition to the patterns hidden in prime numbers. Astronomy particularly exemplifies squeezing maximal information from scarce data.\r\n\r\nConclusion: Both intuition and serendipitous discovery are essential complements to data and theory.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*00:26:52–00:33:32 | AI-Assisted Problem Solving and the Erdős Problems*  \r\nThe discussion covers AI’s mixed success solving Erdős math problems: initial rapid gains by solving “low-hanging fruit” were followed by a plateau. Tao uses a mountain-climbing analogy to describe AI jumping over easier barriers but struggling with deeper, complex hurdles.\r\n\r\nConclusion: AI excels at breadth and brute-force problem tackling but struggles with nuanced partial progress.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*00:33:32–00:36:54 | Complementarity of Human Depth and AI Breadth in Science*  \r\nTerence and the host agree that AI’s strength is breadth, mapping broad fields and easy wins, while human experts focus on depth. Science workflows must adapt to this new model of wide-ranging AI exploration combined with focused human insight.\r\n\r\nConclusion: Future science will be a complementary collaboration, leveraging both AI’s and humans’ unique strengths.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*00:36:54–00:43:42 | Differences Between Programming and Mathematical Research*  \r\nDiscussion about how programming productivity increases with AI differ from math research, as the latter values the deep process of discovery, intuition building, and theory creation, not just results. AI can handle many routine tasks but cannot yet replace core mathematical creativity.\r\n\r\nConclusion: Core intellectual breakthroughs remain human-driven for now, though AI enriches auxiliary work.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*00:43:42–00:49:06 | AI’s Current Limits and Incremental Gains in Mathematics*  \r\nTao emphasizes that AI mostly excels by applying existing techniques and occasionally combining overlooked results rather than inventing fundamentally new math ideas. Success rates are low, but AI’s scale allows picking rare successes, while top math requires new conceptual breakthroughs.\r\n\r\nConclusion: AI is a powerful assistant for existing methods but not yet a source of revolutionary techniques.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*00:49:06–00:56:59 | Intelligence vs. Cleverness and Interactive Problem Solving*  \r\nIntelligence involves cumulative, adaptive progress building upon partial solutions, which AI currently lacks. Present AI relies on trial and error without deep memory or evolving understanding. Tao envisions future mathematicians winnowing and refining AI-generated proofs to find elegance.\r\n\r\nConclusion: Genuine intelligence requires sustained cumulative reasoning—a frontier yet to be reached by AI.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*00:57:00–01:02:27 | Formal Proofs, Narrative Science, and Semi-Formal Languages*  \r\nThe power of formal proof assistants like Lean to break down proofs into atomic steps is discussed, along with the need for semi-formal languages that can integrate narrative and data-based scientific reasoning, enabling better AI-assisted conjecture generation and validation.\r\n\r\nConclusion: Bridging formal and natural scientific discourse is a key challenge to harnessing AI for science progress.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*01:02:27–01:07:53 | The Nature of Conjectures and Scientific Progress Measurement*  \r\nExamples like the prime number theorem illustrate conjectures developed via data and intuition long before formal proofs. The difficulty of quantifying progress in such open-ended tasks is highlighted, as is the challenge of forecasting scientific success without multiple independent histories.\r\n\r\nConclusion: Understanding and measuring scientific progress requires novel frameworks and possibly simulated scientific environments.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*01:07:53–01:16:06 | Serendipity, Scientific Interaction, and Modern Distractions*  \r\nTao reflects on the value of random interactions and accidental discoveries, which are diminished in digitally optimized workflows. Distraction and unstructured time can foster breakthrough thinking, challenging how AI and modern work affect creativity and progress.\r\n\r\nConclusion: Preserving serendipity and unplanned interactions remains vital for creativity in a highly optimized world.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*01:16:06–01:23:11 | The Future of AI and Mathematical Frontiers*  \r\nThoughts on when AI might perform at or beyond Terence Tao's level suggest a near future where many traditional math tasks are AI-assisted or automated, but true frontier breakthroughs require hybrid human-AI collaboration. The evolution of mathematical practice and discovery methods will be profound.\r\n\r\nConclusion: AI will revolutionize math workflows but not supplant the need for human mathematical creativity anytime soon.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n*01:23:11–End | Advice for Early Career Mathematicians in an AI Age*  \r\nTao advises embracing change and adaptability, leveraging new AI tools to contribute earlier than before, and remaining open to new scientific methods. Traditional education remains valuable but should be augmented by novel approaches to keep pace with evolving science landscapes.\r\n\r\nConclusion: Flexibility and openness to new paradigms will be key for success in math careers amid rapid technological change.",

      "text": "Am I the only one here who finds the deliberate and repeated calling of Kepler \"a high temperature LLM\" to be extremely disrespectful, and actually quite disgusting? \nPerhaps guests should opt for visiting ML Street Talk instead of... whatever \"this\" is.",

    {
      "id": "UgzxPse5cRz-6A4DOfh4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "@dwarkeshpatel I realize that I’m commenting 8 days after you posted and the video is now almost 500 comments deep so you may not read this but thanks for a very insightful conversation.  I find Terrance’s take on AI impact to be much more plausible than, say, someone like Alex Wissner-Gross’ continued statements that AI is about to \"bulk solve\" whole fields (biology, physics, math) in one fell swoop in the next 2 years.  Granted that frontier models are improving at fantastic rates and recursive improvement is also accelerating but I also hear Demis noting that there are likely some large as of yet undiscovered strategies between where we’re at now and true super-intelligence AGI.  Recursive alone doesn’t likely get us there.  It may help accelerate but likely alone doesn’t get us there.  Dario and Demis seemed to have some uncertainty on that when I heard them discuss on the Davos stage.  I was more aligned with Demis after that conversation and hearing Terrance talk about the real friction and gaps as it pertains to math reinforced that thought conclusion.  Caveat: everything is moving fast and only time will tell.\r\n\r\nAnother thing I wanted to say was that much of this conversation seemed to focus on standard frontier model capabilities, which is interesting but I would've really liked to hear Terrance's take on whether the Deep Mind protein folding solve process might be instructive as a model for future science.  That was a very targeted domain specific AI in conjunction with an extremely talented team of domain experts which is a different model than just throwing a frontier models en masse at general problems.  It is also true that the protein folding problem was a very quantifiable, well documented problem with a finite solution so this model might not be universally applicable to discovering new frontier science but it does seem that something like this might be the way.  As Terrance was noting, we need to rethink how we do science generally given how fundamentally AI has changed the available toolkit.  I also wonder about the impact of quantum computing plus AI as this seems like another order of magnitude in capability on the reasonably near term horizon. \r\n\r\nThat last topic of How Terry uses his time made me think that one brain with multiple deep domain expertise is another possible lever / order of magnitude unlock. Coupling deep math domain expertise with deep biology expertise for instance might synthesize solutions that would've been unconsidered otherwise. Also, on How Terry uses his time: my vote would be putting Demis and Terrance in a room for a few weeks and letting them noodle on the AI-applied-to-science problem together - that would be amazing. 🧠⚡\n\r\nI do think the path forward is complementary interaction of digital intelligences and biological intelligences where the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. I use \"digital intelligences\" here intentionally as, especially in this context, “artificial” seems wrong.  Going forward, it seems like we will have two different types of intelligence, biological and digital and learning how to interact and co-create seems like the challenge of the future.  Things like speeding the information exchange between the two, building new paradigms that leverage the power of the two together seems a valuable path to at least explore.. It's my most hopeful path for the future. \r\n\r\nThe last bit on how new math students might think about the future in this \"particularly unpredictable era\" as Terrance captioned it is also something I’ve been thinking about in my role as a data center solutions architect.  It’s a relevant question to any cognitively intense knowledge work role going forward.  I do feel like logic and thinking architecturally in frameworks will continue to provide high value.  These skills may even increase in value in the near future.  I think human value will become more about capability than role. \"How I think, how I decide, how I relate, what I protect\" survives role collapse. \"What I do\" doesn't.\r\n\r\nThe other strategy/framework I’ve been deploying is “Cadence over conclusions”. This is the meta-answer to most of my long term future planning right now: values are long-term, plans are short-term, rules are conditional, systems are designed for revision. At current rates of change, weekly/monthly/quarterly/annual reassessment cadence is required and calibrated so that I’m not constantly scanning but also not drifting away from the center of mass that is moving and changing fast.\r\n\r\nIn general, I’ve fallen back on stoicism and controlling the controllables, but with a focus on which levers / controllables actually move the odds. Under AGI uncertainty, most of those levers turn out to be internal — psychological flexibility, identity stability, relational optionality, and the discipline not to over-commit when you can't see far enough ahead to justify it.\r\n\r\nLong comment I know – this interview sent me into deep thought as many of yours do.  You are one of the sources of information that I highly value currently as a virtual lighthouse helping illuminate the path ahead.  You bring in thought leaders and have the chops to ask the right questions and the patience to listen.  It is greatly appreciated.",

      "text": "Что-что, а идеи я генерирую исключительно собственным мозгом. Нейросети не генерируют их за меня.       "id": "UgzAVQeJQgnB_E7lWN54AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "What Tao says about Ptolemy vs Copernicus confirms Kuhn and perfectly retorts against Standard vs Neo-Tychonic. Models, though, are not what's really at stake: core philosophical commitments are.\n\nContrary to popular disinformation, all scientists worth their salt (notably Einstein, Hubble, Hawking and Ellis among many others) have known and admitted, albeit begrudgingly, that a geocentric universe has never been disproven or falsified empirically and is even physically viable,\n\nIn fact, once elliptic orbits had been integrated into the tychonian model, all alleged observational and explanatory advantage of copernican heliocentrism over geocentrism had been progressively eroded and had hit zero by the time of Mach.\n\nThat's why Michelson and Morley felt compelled to prove the Earth's motion around the Sun experimentally via the interferometer, so as to give heliocentrism a decisive edge.\n\nAnd that's why their massive failure became the scientific community's worst nightmare for 24 years — the prospect that the pope could have been right all along was worse than death to them. Einstein was no exception.\n\nHe saved the day by ruling out ether not observationally but conceptually, only to somehow reintroduce it 10 years later in a different form within GR to rescue SR from its inadequacies.\n\nMichelson instead, based on his unwavering belief in the original ether, went on to use the interferometer to measure the rotational motion, too — and this time around it worked. Therefore, the logical implication of ether + no revolution + rotation is: the Earth is at rest at the center, while the Sun and the whole universe revolve around her daily.\n\nThe Standard Model must rely on 95% unobservables in order to be able to claim explanatory power on 5% observables — not exactlly the scientific standard. So much for parsimony and elegance.\n\nCosmic deep time depends, among other things, on Einstein's Isotropic Synchrony Convention about light speed and is integral to the Standard Model and its failed prediction that JWST would observe population III galaxies — what we've got instead is systematic observation of fully mature galaxies in every quadrant of the cosmological horizon, just as publicly predicted by Jason Lisle, consistent with his already proposed Anisotropic Synchrony Convention, whereby we see the universe live and not back in time. \n\nMoreover, unlike gravitational entropy, thermodynamic entropy is observed and works directly against overall spontaneous complex information generation and order formation, i.e. against any type of large-scale evolution, whether cosmic or biological, therefore deep-time thinking is antiscientific backward reasoning, and injecting more deep time by some sleight of hand such as by constantly tweaking down Hubble's constant is all the more silly — it just makes things worse.\n\nStandard stellar formation theory doesn't work physically and displays circular reasoning; Earth and moon formation theories don't work either; Nasa sent probes to measure the Earth's and some of our planets' allegedly old magnetic fields, only to be proven wrong by Russell Humphreys, who back in the '80s had been accurate in his public prediction of how young they'd be found to be; from the '70s up until at least 2024, peer-reviewed papers have reported evidence of periodic distribution, at every observable scale, of galaxies, quasars and gamma-ray bursts in concentric shells with Earth at their center; so far, three generations of probes have detected, every more clearly, large-scale anisotropies in the CMB and, correspondingly, universe-wide alignments with the Earth's ecliptic and equator, again in direct violation of the so-called cosmological (aka so-called copernican aka mediocrity aka antigeocentric) principle.\n\nAt the geological level, Z-pinch-generated radioactive heavy elements display native parent-daughter ratios identical to those found in rocks, thus falsifying the core assumption behind geologic deep-time radiometry, whereas radiocarbon is systematically found throughout the geologic column (whose contiguous layers btw are all erosion-free and full of polystrate fossils despite being allegedly laid down millions of years apart from one another), as well as in dinosaur bones (along with 16 different types of soft tissue), diamonds, coal and oil deposits; and there's way too much helium in zircons for them to be old.\n\nAt the biological level, deep time is precluded by real-world cross-species data, such as demographic growth rates, fast mutation rates vs low variation, unintended findings via DNA barcoding and the fundamentally deleterious nature of virtually all mutations, most of which are tiny, go unselected, fixate in the populations and degrade the species' genomes, putting shelf-lives on them - and by the same token, the process has not been going on for long.\n\nWe do live in a young and Earth-centered universe, it's just that you guys are so biased and have over the centuries grown too used to running from it and suppressing the evidence because you are too scared of the obvious implications.",

      "id": "UgxfSSqRGfDrVhCNoEZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I'm not sure idea generation has had its cost reduced much, in particular good ideas. These models at least in my experience do not come up with any good ideas. You can try to discuss ideas with them, they kinda stink at that, they are best at doing handheld reviews, so you can look for sources without knowing about them, and you can guide an AI through a discussion for the purposes of reviewing it yourself.\n\nYes these model makes it easier for people to form their ideas in a more presentable way, but the majority of it is still garbage. I would say even most ideas that come from professors are garbage to begin with.  \n\nWhat we need is better models that can actually do serious review, both to facilitate better workflow in idea generation, to filter out bad ideas earlier, and enabke more people to catch their mistakes earlier, but also to facilitate review itself. \n\nThe danger is that the models will never really work properly and will get bogged down in a library of dogma that they create. \n\nSomething like automated labs would be a good idea, overseen by humans maybe, but capable of running experiments. In particular running replication studies and to do independent new tests of equipment or statistical assumptions in that process of review. \n\nI think that kind of thing could be essential in physics, if we are going to scale research, and to actually run replication across an increasing volume of research. \n\nLets say you are interested in anti correlation experiments, or entanglement experiments, but you are skeptical of the results, maybe because of unknowns in detector physics, maybe you want to run further independent tests of equipment, maybe you want more runs, or to modify the setups, and run replication with scrutiny, then an automated lab where you can interact with and see the setups, test the setups, get proper documentation on the components used and so forth, and then you can actually run a replication study in a day or two by just booking a workbench. \n\nAnd developing such labs, with all sorts of equipment, could eventually facilitate better models in running their own experiments. I really think something like this will be necessary for any AI model to be able to escape our bubble of accumilated knowledge and dogma.",
      "like_count": 0,

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "21:00 \"Right now we're going through a cognitive version of the Copernican revolution where we used to think that human intelligence is the center of the universe.\"\n\nQuantum physics states that consciousness and perception are necessary for Reality to be defined, observed, or even exist.\n\nTherefore, I believe that everyone is at the center of the universe that they are experiencing and perceiving.",
      "like_count": 1,

      "author": "@hanleyk",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/T5u74rs4R66je7_-bDsjCmQn93HlgaHdwmjvvT9TWUXHaB6Er5t_7wOTDsFxlIKxSs83Y5yImQ0=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgyczLbMGwURwspYgEx4AaABAg",
      "text": "One difference between belief and science is pointing out precisely why a conclusion necessarily stems from premises. You seem to miss that still:\n\nWhere in the mathematics does it say that consciousness and perception are necessary for reality? That would be your premise. Please precisely state this (i.e. with equations, not words).\n\nThen, why would this imply that humans are at the center of the universe? Please formally define the center of the universe (again, use equations) and then define what you mean by humans in this framework. \n\nFinally, show me exactly why these two conceptualisations are connected. If you fail to do any of these it may be worthwhile to restrict your potentially spurious beliefs and sharpen your training in mathematics and physics?",

    {
      "id": "UgwgCMXeyGpEnXWFdQ14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "17:12 I really like this point because I think it highlights that pretty much everything useful that comes out of these systems is innovation in execution and building architecture around a concept. We can spiral around ideas forever but unless we built on top of them they are forever useless. English is a wonderful achievement, but as a language is constructed is extremely weak axioms. \n\nNow, on this topic, I would further like to highlight that great axioms are built to represent their functions well. With a good abstract vision of the systems your need to build, it’s possible craft an axiom that well represents the concepts and is well equipped to be built upon.\n\nTake e. The number itself can be built from the simple idea of “make a number that is self derivative using an infinite polynomial”. It’s constructed with a clear mechanism and it’s definition is its function. Now it has gone so far beyond in its applicability because of the robustness of its definition, how well it supports the idea that it can be built upon.\n\nComing back to Keplar and AI. The final laws are the hard work and genius, and the datapoints are verifiability. The impressive part is the fact that Keplar could view - abstractly - the motions in concept, and then built solid functional axioms that let him accurately represent that motion. It’s not trying 600 random things until 1 think fits the data. \n\nThat way, we can overfit literally any curve in any datapoint. It would verify 100% of the time, but provides no abstract benefit beyond the sample set. That’s because it’s not making useful inferences about the nature of the data, only the that actual data. It’s not building a good axiom that supports ideas, it’s just building an axiom until it supports the 1 idea which is to verify the results.\n\nWould love to hear more thoughts on this but I do think the idea that Keplar was randomly searching without making serious observations and intuition about the nature of the data is extremely reductive and disrespectful to the craft, effort, and creative thinking that went into producting something robust that extends beyond the immediate requirement.\n\nWith just a few datapoints, he built something that was so much more true than just the data that it came with. It boiled down the massive dataframe into a few key ideas and principles that guided the whole dataset - actually not that dataset, it guided that thing that the dataset represents. We’re not trying to make our work fit the data, we’re trying to use the data to help us understand the underlying context of what the data represents. I’m not a fan of focusing so much on the steps that we forget what we’re even doing in the first place",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCJQnRZ6CQHY5Qu1xmqCpwFw",
      "author": "@EvilNinja182",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/LSbzarUarCnIJAHYmjMZa5hpKvphZMjLN1QoGZmT5hOs8zerpD7rEf4YPUzyGqfQ9NEetN1YOw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "Terence Tao one of the goats!",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/82TCZN3O3aTp6x-ESYHXUYsg_LxXPYrx8z_WFs5mRkkz14aG1_81wj75FUv_hv5k2ywmDbz_=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugz8PmN1qGJ9h2hN1uF4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Tao is right that verification is the new bottleneck. But it’s more tractable than it looks.\n\nThe mistake is running the old sequence: generate → verify → assess value. That made sense when ideas were scarce. They aren’t anymore.\n\nFlip it. Generate → filter for coherence → rank by novelty → verify only what survives.\n\nCoherence filtering is largely solved, formal proof checkers already do it. Novelty scoring is measurable: unexpected cross-domain connections, generalizations of settled results, contradictions of established assumptions. \n\nNovelty correlates historically with significance and doesn’t require subjective judgment.\n\nHuman reviewers can work a prioritized queue instead of an undifferentiated flood. Expert attention can be concentrated where it matters most.\n\nOne safeguard: a small channel reserved for results that score poorly on everything but feel anomalous. That’s how you catch the next Ramanujan instead of filtering him out.\n\nThe finish line isn’t automated verification. It’s a triage system that makes human verification sustainable at machine-generated volume. \n\nThat system is buildable now. The race has an entry point. Almost nobody is standing at it.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCCRDiaNLR7jS0svDYTLNKPQ",

      "text": "Speaking of random ideas with zero actual backing.       "text": " @Michael_CurioMaps  yeah, well i have a phd in computer science from stanford and my success rate on hard new problems is about 0% so i'm impressed by2%. but i think that what matters is not 2% or 10% or 1%. it's the rate fo progress that matters. it's the fact that 2% was unthinkable two years ago. and this space is nuanced enough that there are always reasons to tell yourself that it's over. 2% is far as it gets. good reasons for arguing. but the best counter argument is that those same reasons said we wouldn't break out of 0%. they said we'd get a gold in the olympiad. but the recent track record of good reasons to has been very good.",

      "id": "UgzpxlPhkDtmZPDw8FV4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Overview\nIn this interview, Terence Tao discusses how artificial intelligence is reshaping the landscape of mathematical research and scientific discovery. He explores the philosophical differences between how humans and AI solve problems, the changing bottlenecks in science, and how he personally integrates AI tools into his daily workflow.\n\nKey Themes & Takeaways\nAI is Like Kepler, Not Newton [04:12]\nPatel and Tao use the history of astronomy as an analogy for AI's current capabilities. Johannes Kepler discovered the laws of planetary motion by blindly testing mathematical relationships against massive datasets for decades. Decades later, Isaac Newton provided the unifying theory of gravity to explain why these laws worked. Similarly, modern AI is excellent at finding empirical regularities and generating hypotheses from massive data (like Kepler), but it still lacks the deep, unifying reasoning capabilities of a Newton.\n\nThe New Bottleneck in Science [12:17]\nTraditionally, the hardest part of science was \"idea generation.\" AI has driven the cost of generating hypotheses down to almost zero. The new bottleneck is verification and validation. With AI generating thousands of potential theories daily, human scientists and peer-review systems are becoming overwhelmed trying to figure out which ideas actually represent true, fruitful progress.\n\nAI's Current Plateau in Mathematics [30:33]\nTao notes that while AI recently solved about 50 of the 1,100 open \"Erdős problems,\" it has seemingly hit a plateau after picking the low-hanging fruit. He compares AI to a \"jumping robot\" in a dark mountain range: it can blindly leap incredibly high to reach isolated ledges that humans can't, but it fails to build a cumulative, logical path up the mountain like human climbers do.\n\nBreadth vs. Depth [35:20]\nCurrent AI models excel at breadth—they can apply standard techniques to millions of problems simultaneously. Humans excel at depth. Tao envisions a future where AI broadly maps out new fields and solves all the tedious, surface-level problems, leaving the deeply complex \"islands of difficulty\" for human experts to tackle.\n\nHow Tao Personally Uses AI [47:09]\nTao states that AI has changed the style of his work rather than the core of it. AI tools allow him to easily generate complex code, create visualizations, format his papers, and do deep literature reviews—tasks that would have taken hours before. However, for the most difficult, core aspects of solving a new math problem, he still relies on traditional pen and paper.\n\nArtificial Cleverness vs. Intelligence [49:27]\nTao draws a distinction between current AI and true intelligence. When two human mathematicians collaborate, they build a cumulative understanding, adaptively improving their ideas as they bounce thoughts off one another. Current LLMs lack this ability; they rely on brute-force trial and error and cannot retain or build upon new abstract skills organically during a session.\n\nAdvice for the Next Generation [01:21:09]\nBecause AI is lowering the barrier to entry (e.g., allowing high schoolers to contribute to frontier math using formal proof assistants like Lean), Tao advises young mathematicians to cultivate high adaptability. The old paradigm of spending decades merely learning existing math before contributing is changing, so students must embrace curiosity, non-traditional learning paths, and massive technological shifts.",

Science and mathematics will use it to solve entirely new classes of problems and invent new paradigms that make use of it's strengths. I'm most interested in how it'll change biology because that's a field where breadth is essential and deep theories not so much.",

      "id": "UgzhOdqE8-514HrsO_V4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Professor Tao precisely captures the current limitation of AI by describing it as a \"stochastic jumping machine.\" The root cause of these hallucinations and the inability to accumulate deep, multi-step reasoning lies in the unbounded nature of the search space itself—a blind spot inherited from standard Zermelo-Fraenkel Set Theory (ZFC). Standard ZFC permits infinite, unconstrained phase spaces where stochastic continuous searches inevitably diverge or produce \"slop.\"\n\nIf we approach intelligence through the rigorous lens of mathematical physics, any physically realizable information channel must have a finite capacity. It must be \"trace-class\" (or nuclear), meaning the sum of its singular values must be strictly finite (Σ s_n < ∞). This points toward a necessary paradigm shift: a \"Nuclear ZFC\" (NZFC) framework. By enforcing spectral compactness and a strict trace-norm budget as governing boundary conditions, we can collapse the infinite optimization space into discrete, arithmetically rigid pathways. True AI might not emerge from simply scaling up compute in an unbounded continuous space, but rather from recognizing the fundamental topological limits of information itself.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "In Reductionist systems, such as most Sciences, you start with a problem.\nIn Holistic Systems you start with the data and worry about the questions later.\n\nThree major Holistic software systems are Databases, WebSearch, and LLMs. There are many others.\nAll AIs and all humans are Holistic at the bottom.       "id": "Ugxio-hH0p87My4QlFx4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "At [51:24], the Dwarkesh points out a perceived flaw: If Claude, CGPT or Gemini solves a gnarly problem, the model itself hasn't actually \"learned\" anything because as soon as you open a new session, its memory is wiped. Tao agrees, noting it lacks the cumulative, adaptive \"cleverness\" of two human mathematicians bouncing ideas off each other and building intuition.\n\nIt's called a context window! Saying AI isn't truly intelligent because it forgets the conversation when you hit \"refresh\" is like saying a human isn't intelligent because they don't know anything before they're born. It's confusing the inference phase with the training phase.\n\nIn the educational sphere of Machine Learning, we call this the difference between frozen weights and active training. When AI systems are deployed in self-play loops (like AlphaGo or the newer reinforcement-learning reasoning models), they absolutely do build cumulative understanding. They generate synthetic data, evaluate their own proofs, update their neural weights, and come back smarter. They don't just solve the problem; they shift the entire baseline of their understanding. By the time the next model drops, the \"intuition\" Tao is looking for has been baked directly into the neural architecture.\n\nAt [01:18:04], Tao predicts that within a decade, AI will handle the bulk of what goes into math papers, but humans will just move on to some new, elusive \"core\" of what math really is.\n\nIt’s the classic moving goalpost! Every time a computer does something impossible, whether it's beating Garry Kasparov at chess, folding proteins, or solving 50 Erdős problems, someone will say, \"Well, that wasn't real intelligence. That was just a calculator on steroids.\"\n\nThe reality is, the AI isn't just formatting our parentheses or acting as a glorified search engine. It is rapidly climbing the cognitive ladder. Right now, it's acting as a hyper-competent research assistant. But tomorrow? It’s writing the synthesis , reviewing it, publishing it, and complaining about the airline peanuts on the flight to Stockholm to collect the Nobel. That's the deal with AI!",

      "id": "UgzWOgK7IFXxvC5kzzJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "What is the deal with the world’s smartest people underestimating AI? I watch this interview with Terence Tao, a math genius, the Mozart of Math and he’s talking about artificial intelligence like it’s a very eager, highly educated golden retriever that occasionally finds a tennis ball in the bushes. He’s looking at the greatest technological paradigm shift in human history, and he’s saying, \"Eh, it's a good co-author. It formats my parentheses.\"\n\nRight around [33:02], Tao compares modern AI to a \"jumping machine\" in a dark mountain range. He says it can randomly leap two meters in the air and clear low walls, but it can't systematically rock-climb a 15-foot cliff because it lacks the ability to make \"partial progress.\"\n\nBut here’s the thing, people: If you have a billion jumping robots, you don't need to rock climb! You just build a staircase out of the robots!\n\nTao is applying a very human constraint—the necessity of sequential, step-by-step depth—to an entity that operates on infinite breadth. At [35:26], he admits AI excels at breadth while humans excel at depth. But in computer science, specifically with massive parallel compute and Reinforcement Learning, sufficient breadth becomes depth. If an AI can instantaneously simulate a billion different \"two-meter jumps\" in the latent space of a mathematical problem, the statistical probability of chaining those jumps into a cohesive path to the top of the 15-foot cliff approaches 100%. We aren't just sending one robot to jump in the dark; we are illuminating the entire mountain range with compute.\n\nEarly in the video, the interviewer makes this great analogy [04:12]: Kepler was basically a high-temperature Large Language Model. He spent 20 years staring at Brahe’s astronomical data, wildly guessing geometric shapes, playing with platonic solids, until he empirically \"hallucinated\" the laws of planetary motion. Then, a century later, Isaac Newton comes along—the deep, deductive human—and explains why it works using gravity.\n\nTao uses this to imply that AI will just generate the \"slop\" (the hypotheses), and we will always need the human \"Newton\" to filter it, verify it, and build the deep theoretical framework.\n\nBut why are we assuming the AI stops at Kepler? The only reason Kepler couldn't do what Newton did was a lack of underlying data and compute (his own brain). An AI that can find the empirical regularity in seconds is fundamentally capable of abstracting the inverse-square law in the next token generation. AI isn't just a brute-force statistical engine; modern architectures are already mapping deductive logic. It doesn't just find the pattern; it compresses the pattern into a generalized law. The AI isn't waiting for Newton; the AI is Newton, just running at a clock speed we can't comprehend.",

      "id": "UgwkEVXVFqo7_yMH_Ep4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Since I use agentic AI, I have become a much more hardcore AI user, however, I feel there still seems to be issues with \"learning\" on the job, e.g. the solutions \"we\" find manifest differently in my thinking than that of the agent. While the agent can make notes and load them, I feel there is this productivity peak at 60-70% of the context window that is lost, when the first context compression takes place. And the state is usually quite unique, it cannot just be reproduced neither from the agent's notes, nor from my guidance. I feel while it is difficult for me to get all the details in my working memory, which seems simple for the Agent, this difficult to describe creative state I can reenter more readily than the agent.",

      "id": "UgzkZdb5y9DXti4QXet4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "False.  It has opened up so many opportunities for new ideas and is so overwhelming that it APPEARS (to the non technical mind like Tao) as if new ideas generation is no longer needed or valued.\n\nOn the contrary, with AI, all those ideas that used to be \"impossible\" now become possible.  I just takes a certain mindset to see it.\n\nI'll give you an example.\n\nHow many of you thought that with AI, using tools like claude code, that you could build for yourself, without even know how to code, a full fledged AI powered Home budgeting app, or a living in retirement app, or a travel planning app, that incorporates all of your bank statements, debit/credit card usage, your preferences, teaching it over time, can scan the internet for the best deals, and you can literally architect an AI powered app that SURPRISES you and allows you to live a life optimally knowing you got the best deals available?\n\nTao is just manifesting being threatened by AI, as it is true, AI will eventually be able to CREATE new mathematical discoveries, so his job is eventually going to become deprecated, but, with all that no longer needed work, there is still 24 hours in a day, and with that extra time, you can leverage AI to produce new ideas you never thought were possible for you!\n\nAI is the greatest human invention ever in history, and it's not even close.",

      "id": "UgwlWC6ia12wEAoGKtp4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Tao seemed clearly uncomfortable with the way you described Kepler as if he were simply “trying random things.” That makes Kepler sound arbitrary or careless, which is misleading. Before he had the decisive observational data, Kepler was already working within a serious mathematical and astronomical project: he was trying to uncover an underlying order in planetary motion. His early ideas were speculative, but they were not random. What made his work decisive was that, once confronted with precise observations, he kept revising those models until they matched the data.",

      "text": "What is amazing is that the measurements made optically by Tycho didn't contain a lot of errors to throw off Kepler. Otherwise the law wouldn't have lasted so long.",

    {
      "id": "UgwZT77Ynj1iKiFs13J4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Given how AI is static after training on big data, it should not be a surprise what it can and cannot do;\nit is prompted, then based upon the prompt, it travels the static high dimensional space crystallized in training,\nthen an answer comes out. \n  This way \"convergent\" intelligence will be soon solved with these models, but they cannot do novelty that cannot directly be deduced from the sum of the prompt and the static high dimensional space.\n  I think these questions would be very important to discuss because this would allow for a healthier understanding and application of AI.",

      "author_id": "UC99OF6-7ZzXvvbXLiFxinqA",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "1:19:34 while i really like these podcasts and the people he has on, i think Dwarkesh is a bit too enamored of the vague 'datacenter of geniuses' earning trillions of dollars (from…what?) being the end goal of humanity, and the only question is on what date we hit that magical threshold.",

      "parent": "UgxvmEjxMetpmb4EYgB4AaABAg",
      "text": "indeed , i agree , he asked some better more open ended questions like about what an intermediary language for conjecture might look like or the process of being able to learn a diverse amount of domains . but then its fairly insulting of Dwarkesh to so bluntly ask \"when will this replace you\" its like he wasnt listening to all the nuance Tao stated about what goes into actually contributing to science and collaborating and the clear differences in our abilities and expertise compared to computation .  neural networks are incredible , and incredibly alien to human processes , thats a GOOD thing , we make much better collaborators with a diverse forms of \"intelligence\" .",

    {
      "id": "Ugyab3RrHJ3C8hvDIfl4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Re Dwarkesh's question at 51:11, theorem provers like Lean are taking advantage of correspondance between Type Theories and systems of Formal Logic (the correspondence is bigger then that but that isnt important here) called the Curry-Howard Correspondance. For every system of formal logic you have a type theory and vice versa. For example Propositional Logic corresponds to Simply Typed Lambda Calculus. Richer Type Theories correspond to richer logical systems. Lean 4 is based on the Calculus of Inductive Constructions which has full dependent types (Sigma and Pi) plus quotients and a bunch of other stuff (and is Non-Constructive unfortunately imo). This allows you to model vast areas of logic and math.\n\nWhen you construct a \"proof\" in a theorem prover you are literally writing a type that corresponds to the statement you want to prove and then you write a term that inhabits that type. The existence of the term constitutes the proof. \n\nFor example, Modus Ponens `(P ^ P=>Q) => Q` maps directly to typing judgment for function application in Simply Typed Lambda Calculus:\n\nap : A -> (A -> B) -> B\nap a f = f a\n\nSo when Dwarkesh asks if the proofs coming from Lean are going to be human readable, the answer is that they must at least isomorphic to a human readable proof. At the end of the day they will be a giant composition of functions where different functions describe lemmas that build up to your final proof. You can mechanically trip away the terms and translate the types into statements in the corresponding system of formal logic. It likely wont be as neat and orderly as a human written proof and will have an \"assembly langugae\" vibe but it will be readable by someone invested in understanding it.",
      "like_count": 3,
      "author_id": "UCVAP2MQee7Sr_OOkefvbo-w",
      "author": "@ICopiedJohnOswald",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "In order for AI to be a partner it needs to be able to know what it doesn't know. It needs to be able to question, and for that, it needs to be able to doubt. The most frustrating thing about frontier models is how they need to be told to research, or use a tool, or what have you.",

    {
      "id": "UgyDUtpcpaKXyU3_N_V4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "This podcast, like the Karpathy and Ilya Sutskever interview, hints at the single most important thing missing from LLMs - the ability to evaluate partial results. The current paradigm allows models to solve tasks that are fully verifiable and completed, but models have no way to make and evaluate incremental progress towards solutions. Once they can do that, then suddenly reinforcement can be applied not just to problem solving but to theory building, problem creation and I suspect most other domains. And I think continual learning and full generality might follow soon after.",
      "like_count": 9,
      "author_id": "UCUTM7_FUhtGoozECVxwVDSQ",
      "author": "@pianoforte611",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lvXB9vuj0A9vL2DU9S7F6D3t6LXpZbIXt-1UuM3Kl1nA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 weeks ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1774137600,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyDUtpcpaKXyU3_N_V4AaABAg.AUaYABwmam9AUa_KoGT2BR",
      "parent": "UgyDUtpcpaKXyU3_N_V4AaABAg",
      "text": "The difference between a partial result and a dead end can be exceedingly difficult to detect, until you have a full result to cast retrospective clarity. Even in the case of self-contained lemmas, if your lemmas multiply like lemmings, you only end up making your combinatorial search worse than ever. Whether we can automate the separation of the potent lemmas from the impotent lemmas remains an open research problem. \n\n\"once they can do that\" skipped the proof step that you are not talking about an empty set. This is why they set up peer review to screen out amateurs. \n\nSo many times in math: If you had an object with properties X, Y and Z, you could work miracles. Usually this means that objects with all those properties are non-existent.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UC5khRFNWuwVQmuFRf5z6Zdw",
      "author": "@afterthesmash",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nzf_38osY0eh7aPQbfKu6wRof-DTAs7pSaNm9ZMqGPUJFfWyS5SFzzSHFBOz2qGsV8gw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgxtvNOAlKu5fp9oeQ94AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Trit would be ternary versus binary which actually is mathematically the ideal computer science model for machine code processing. I think at 3 values (-1, 0, 1) the utility average mathematically comes out to about 1.51 versus i think about .89 (my memory may be off) of the bit (0, 1).  Counterintuitive though is the fact as you go beyond ternary (4 values per bit or more) the optimization average actually starts to go down further and further. There is already software logic that utilizes ternary for efficiency but we really need to put some effort into raw silicone if we want to see that roughly 80% effective efficiency improvement really come to fruition.  I really do foresee it happening in to the near future as it could likely have MASSIVE impacts at scale in data centers or chained computer modeling.",

      "id": "UgwgcSG-om1cHsO3bOZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "LLMs are good at finding answers, but how good are they at finding better questions?\nThe logic of language is very different than the logic of mathematics, and computer science.\nIn natural language, we refer to reality, the universe, truth, concepts too broad for mathematics.\nAlso, we refer to contradictions, paradoxes, ambiguities in natural language, that mathematics rejects.\n\nDoes an LLM understand a transcendent truth that mathematics doesn't capture?\nFor example, (4<3) is not a true statement.\nHowever, (4<3 is not a true statement) is a true statement.\nTruth is ambiguous is a true statement not treatable by mathematics. (It's stating the nature of the problem.)\nHowever, a tautology, or a symmetry, or an axiomatic system is treatable by mathematics.\n\nIt seems that LLMs do the job of disambiguation, on some level it must treat the problem of too much meaning for too few words.\nIt seems that an LLM that asks its own questions and develops its own vocabulary in an impromptu manner would be far more powerful, especially treating the problem of ambiguity.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCStBfbqbQisPmqAZIH6IhEg",
      "author": "@ywtcc",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/MZtcsk1mXP3oc2SWlLydcAtbBf8MWItCX1fkjZLrTihLSTy1K1tU2kNQGjfT4VLcGXnTvy--=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 weeks ago",
      "timestamp": 1774137600,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "6:50 It doesn't hurt to remember that Johannes Kepler struggled with financial stability his entire life. At the same time that he made his discoveries he also had to find work as an astrologist, surveyor, teacher, mathematician, calendar publisher and more, and still finding himself in poverty multiple times; while Tycho Brahe was born wealthy and got sponsored by the king of Denmark. Brahe had every opportunity, all of the data, and all of the tools necessary to make the same discoveries as Kepler, but he didn't.\n\nWe celebrate Johannes Kepler and not Tycho Brahe for the same reason that we value grounded conclusions derived from data more the just the by data itself. It's more useful and tells us more about the workings of the universe.",
      "like_count": 85,
      "author_id": "UCFyYiVYZkfElj5Or2y60YXg",

      "id": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg.AUaCiKkm69PAUatqiAwPCG",
      "parent": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg",

    {

      "text": "​ @fortifiedwall9047  Actually, there is a much more profound difference in this case.     {

      "parent": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg",
      "text": "Resuenan en mí cabeza estás sabias palabras: \"no cualquiera puede ser un genio, pero un genio puede salir de cualquier lado\" no se dónde la escuché pero seguro las dijo Platón",

    {
      "id": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg.AUaCiKkm69PAUbrPI9ADcs",
      "parent": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg",
      "text": "It's weird that you want to justify the celebration of Kepler over Brahe over the former's analytical skills. But Brahe's observational skills and annotational discipline were just as important! Yeah, Brahe could have made the same conclusions as Kepler, but he could have been womanizing with all the wealth and connections he had instead of observing the stars in the middle of the night. He made sacrifices even if he was already interested in astronomy in the first place, and he should be celebrated equally for that.\n\nHe did something remarkable with the privilege he had, let's not judge him or diminish his achievements based on those privileges. There were plenty of other people who were in the same position as him, had the same opportunities or more and could have contributed to astronomy but did not...",
      "like_count": 9,
      "author_id": "UCPCdrbQT4WpcmNFCNgov_2Q",
      "author": "@kevikiru",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/8N5iIJXBnDviQfM1Y7e9_j7ZwAmtVVH_BrhVDwyNwuxE_EpAo9lyl3ClHOc87Klg2E_Uk2aI_w=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 weeks ago",
      "timestamp": 1774137600,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg.AUaCiKkm69PAUc1B2cHZ1g",
      "parent": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg.AUaCiKkm69PAUbrPI9ADcs",
      "text": "​​ @kevikiru  Tycho Brahe was fired for neglect and mismanagement, was widely disliked by his peers, and was accused of infidelity. The data in question is that of planetary motion and therefore very common anytime anywhere; it is best known simply for being the data available to Kepler. \n\nBrahe had been given an island and an observatory built and paid for by Denmark; in addition to his position in the court, he was awarded titles from which taxes could be collected so that he could fund his own pursuits. After being spoiled he became demanding, arrogant, and neglectful, which when added to his excentric and unfaithful behavior, accounts for his fall from the graces of most of the Danish court, and his eventual firing. \n\nIn short, Brahe did use his and other people's wealth irresponsibly, and probably was indeed a womanizer. I don't know how that has anything to do with his data, but the fact is that many others in his position could have done the same thing, because there were indeed many other people doing the same thing, before, after, and at the same time as him. Meanwhile, it is hard to argue that many others could have discovered Kepler's laws. \n\nI have no opinion on the matter of whether Brahe should be celebrated or not; the fact is that he is not, but it is my opinion that Kepler definitely should.\n\nThank you for the opportunity to add more historical context.",
      "like_count": 3,
      "author_id": "UCFyYiVYZkfElj5Or2y60YXg",
      "author": "@Paco96",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_niYpHvNWqlwj4rnUlb3nNTyeok1KdCkqqm2Axq_yZX2A=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "3 weeks ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1774742400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg.AUaCiKkm69PAUc43BwD-6A",
      "parent": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg.AUaCiKkm69PAUc1B2cHZ1g",
      "text": "​ @Paco96 Tao clearly said the data was scarce and essential for Kepler's results, why would you assume detailed data collection on planetary motion would be common?",
      "like_count": 5,
      "author_id": "UCyd9Wdc_l4qLjQ4eiJbffqA",
      "author": "@_mosesb",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/9mqGFTsWxXBKBnWpnjZNQZoW3YVg-OpjIbiCi49epBr3IsiOl3PM20LP2QaLBbEByRHW-Gp4ew=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "3 weeks ago",
      "timestamp": 1774742400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg.AUaCiKkm69PAUcEtyk7LGO",
      "parent": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg.AUaCiKkm69PAUc1B2cHZ1g",
      "text": "It is not an assumption. Perhaps the way in which I typed may have been easily misinterpreted, so allow me to rephrase. People have always been captured by the seemingly erratic movement of planets, hence their name meaning 'wanderer'; this has led people to continuously register data on their movement, sometimes in an effort to find a pattern or better understand it. This fascination is pretty much universal to humanity and therefore, many observations had been made before Brahe, and many have been made since. This means that data on planetary motion is widespread, since it has been registered for so long and in so many places. What Tycho Brahe was pursuing was actually extremely common, that is not an assumption, it is a fact.\n\nThis doesn't mean that Brahe's data was not necessary for Kepler. Actually, Brahe's data was highly accurate and it is therefore hard to say whether Kepler could have discovered the patterns of planets' orbits if he hadn't had access to a small part of Brahe's data; that is what is being referred to in the video. \n\nAlthough, I would argue that since Brahe's observations had been made with the naked eye, and the invention of the telescope was contemporary with Kepler and Brahe which would eventually lead to much accurate data, and with Kepler eventually taking over Brahe's position in Prague, it is somewhat possible that Kepler could have eventually figured it out anyways on his own.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCFyYiVYZkfElj5Or2y60YXg",
      "author": "@Paco96",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_niYpHvNWqlwj4rnUlb3nNTyeok1KdCkqqm2Axq_yZX2A=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "3 weeks ago",
      "timestamp": 1774742400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg.AUaCiKkm69PAUkNVWCZVgd",
      "parent": "UgzAqc3uZzILoxtakyZ4AaABAg.AUaCiKkm69PAUc1B2cHZ1g",
      "text": " @Paco96  Are you this stubborn not to realize that you can celebrate Kepler but still appreciate Tycho for what he did? It seems so personal to you, so may I ask: have you done more that Tycho? If you haven't, then just appreciate him for what he did.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCPCdrbQT4WpcmNFCNgov_2Q",
      "author": "@kevikiru",

    {
      "id": "Ugyb_ED-u1QupYOpxzR4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Terence Tao commenting on how \"efficiency\" isn't always in the interest of progress.  Huh... that's gonna make some amount of people petulantly angry.",
      "like_count": 37,
      "author_id": "UCQimpe7DFyLrRKSZNZyWKLw",
      "author": "@Rockyzach88",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/rpGZ_d04bCQ50cCu4R7ZwvtbmA5OvPu0otzd_Ls_9pVWJ8u6vDtbp1YJQV9a_t6NIwZ-54n6Sig=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "4 weeks ago",
      "timestamp": 1774137600,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugyb_ED-u1QupYOpxzR4AaABAg.AUa2Fovi5ABAV28RHog4OC",
      "parent": "Ugyb_ED-u1QupYOpxzR4AaABAg",
      "text": "It's very forward thinking of him. Efficiency and optimization got us into the 21st century, but it's time to stop worshipping it so much. \"Efficiency\" is a bit of a fool's mistress, especially when you're sacrificing a lot in other areas in order to further optimize your objective by only a few percentage points. Think about oil companies continuing to drill for oil despite lasting damage to the environment, because their metrics of success don't measure the impact to the environment, despite the fact that the damage they are doing costs us much more than whatever worth we are getting from the oil as a species. Efficiency requires some sort of metric to optimize for, but often we don't even know how to measure the things we want to optimize. For instance, how do you measure creativity? If you're not sure, then how could you possibly optimize for it? You'll likely end up optimizing for some surrogate and often end up doing worse, because optimizing your chosen marker to it's absolute peak comes at the cost of sacrificing things you didn't even know were important for what you were really trying to optimize.",
      "like_count": 4,
      "author_id": "UCaSjIVJX3cpMUoF8sMIyszQ",
      "author": "@justindie7543",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mFSpiwUi5gaPWfG9DXTS6grCaRa5dE06KMAuJb5lpA2Js=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "12:15 \"AI has driven the cost of idea generation down to almost zero... but it doesn't create abundance by itself. Now the bottleneck is different.       "text": "Is math a human infention or a discovery ? \n\nUranus wobbled.\n\nThe math said: “There must be exactly one unseen planet here, with this mass, this distance, this motion.”\n\nLe Verrier solved the equations.\nOnly one solution made the wobble disappear.\n\nHe pointed at a blank patch of sky:\n“It’s right there.”\n\nAstronomers looked…\nand Neptune was exactly where the unique solution said it had to be.\n\nNo alternatives.\nThe missing piece was the only piece.\n\nTherefore: truth.",

      "text": "@van @noeu67 I guarantee you there are millions of people in the world who can listen to this video at 2x speed and answer literally any questions you have about the video with high accuracy.  I’ve never encountered information so dense that simply doubling someone’s speaking speed would make it too much.  Speaking speed simply isn’t fast enough to use up all the mental bandwidth by simply doubling it?  If I need to slow down someone’s talking, I probably need to pause. This video is different because I was a professional mathematician so I knew all the mathematical concepts he discussed in here already really well and it didn’t require much attention.  For research lectures and conference talks in completely unrelated areas that I watch, I won’t watch at 2x speed but only to provide myself time to take notes and look things up.       "text": " @kawingchan  \nIn aggregate, that has always been a cost, though\n\nBut in the pre-AI age, somebody like Tao would have faced far more market barrier costs than he does now, and given that his skill set is better suited to identifying which ideas hold the most value than your average person, the relative costs are significantly lower as a matter of structural logistics.\n\nAs a matter of historical precedent, his point is more than valid across a broad range of domains",

      "text": " @noeu67  he never said the ideas are valuable!  how many images are generated by AI per second in the the world that once would have taken illustrators, designers, artists, 3D designers 10s to 100s of hours per idea? # Terence Tao – How the world’s top mathematician uses AI

## Description

We begin the episode with the absolutely ingenious and surprising way in which Kepler discovered the laws of planetary motion.

People sometimes say that AI will make especially fast progress at scientific discovery because of tight verification loops. But the story of how we discovered the shape of our solar system shows how the verification loop for correct ideas can be decades (or even millennia) long.

During this time, what we know today as the better theory can often actually make worse predictions (Copernicus's model of circular orbits around the sun was actually less accurate than Ptolemy's geocentric model). And the reasons it survives this epistemic hell is some mixture of judgment and heuristics that we don’t even understand well enough to actually articulate, much less codify into an RL loop.

Hope you enjoy!
