It sounds like you don't think the bottleneck&nbsp;&nbsp; in science is finding more things that&nbsp; are the equivalent of the third law of&nbsp;&nbsp; planetary motion for each given field,&nbsp; so that later on somebody can say, "Oh,&nbsp;&nbsp;

we need a way to explain this. Let's work out the&nbsp; math. Here's the inverse-square law of gravity."&nbsp; I think AI has driven the cost of&nbsp; idea generation down to almost zero,&nbsp;&nbsp; in a very similar way to how the internet drove&nbsp;

the cost of communication down to almost zero.&nbsp; It’s an amazing thing, but it doesn't create&nbsp; abundance by itself. Now the bottleneck is&nbsp;&nbsp; different. We're now in a situation where&nbsp; suddenly people can generate thousands of&nbsp;&nbsp;

theories for a given scientific problem. Now we have to verify them, evaluate them.&nbsp; This is something which we have to change our&nbsp; structures of science to actually sort this&nbsp;&nbsp; out. Traditionally, we build walls. In the past,&nbsp;

before we had AI slop, we had amateur scientists&nbsp;&nbsp; have their own theories of the universe,&nbsp; many of which were of very little value.&nbsp; We built these peer review publication&nbsp; systems to filter out and try to isolate&nbsp;&nbsp;

the high signal ideas to test. But now that we can generate these&nbsp;&nbsp; possible explanations at massive scale, and&nbsp; some of them are good and a lot are terrible,&nbsp;&nbsp; human reviewers are already being overwhelmed.

Many journals are reporting that AI-generated&nbsp;&nbsp; submissions are just flooding their submissions. It's great that we can generate all kinds of&nbsp;&nbsp; things now with AI, but it means that the rest&nbsp; of the aspects of science have to catch up:&nbsp;&nbsp;

verification, validation, and assessing&nbsp; what ideas actually move the subject forward&nbsp;&nbsp; and which ones are dead ends or red herrings. That's not something we know how to do at scale.&nbsp; For each individual paper, we can&nbsp;

have a debate among scientists&nbsp;&nbsp; and get to a consensus in a few years. But when we're generating a thousand of&nbsp;&nbsp; these every day, this doesn't work. There's this incredibly interesting&nbsp;&nbsp;

question. If you have billions of AI&nbsp; scientists, not only how do you gauge&nbsp;&nbsp; which ones are real progress, but how do you... This is actually a question that human science&nbsp;&nbsp; has had to face and we've solved somehow,&nbsp;

and I’m actually not sure how we solved this.&nbsp; Let's say in the 1940s, if you're at Bell Labs&nbsp; and there are these new technologies coming out.&nbsp; Pulse-code modulation, how do you transfer&nbsp; signals? How do you digitize signals?&nbsp;&nbsp;

How do you transfer them over analog wires? There are all these papers about the engineering&nbsp;&nbsp; constraints and the details, and then there's one&nbsp; which comes up with the idea of the bit, which has&nbsp;&nbsp; implications across many different fields.

You need some system which can then look&nbsp;&nbsp; at that and say, "Okay, we need&nbsp; to apply this to probability.&nbsp; We need to apply this to&nbsp; computer science," et cetera.&nbsp;

In the future, the AIs are coming up with&nbsp; the next version of this unifying concept.&nbsp; How would you identify it among millions of papers&nbsp; that might actually constitute progress, but which&nbsp;&nbsp; have much less in terms of general unifying ideas?

A lot of it's the test of time.&nbsp; Many great ideas didn't actually get a great&nbsp; reception at the time they were first proposed.&nbsp; It was only after some other scientists&nbsp; realized that they could take it further&nbsp;&nbsp;

and apply them to their own... Deep learning itself was a&nbsp;&nbsp; niche area of AI for a long time. The idea of getting answers entirely&nbsp;&nbsp; through training on data and not through first&nbsp;

principles reasoning was very controversial,&nbsp;&nbsp; and it just took a long time before it started&nbsp; bearing fruit. You mentioned the bit. There were&nbsp;&nbsp; other proposals for computer architectures&nbsp; than the zero-one that is universal today.&nbsp;

I think there were trits, three-valued logic. In an alternate universe,&nbsp;&nbsp; maybe a different paradigm would have shown up. The transformer, for example, is the foundation of&nbsp;&nbsp; all modern large language models, and it was the&nbsp;

first deep learning architecture that really was&nbsp;&nbsp; sophisticated enough to capture language. But it didn't have to be that way.&nbsp; There could've been some other architecture that&nbsp; was the first to do it and once that was adopted,&nbsp;&nbsp;

it would become the standard. One reason why it's hard to&nbsp;&nbsp; assess whether a given idea is going to be&nbsp; fruitful is that it depends on the future.&nbsp; It depends also on the culture and society,&nbsp;

which ones get adopted, which ones don't.&nbsp; The base ten numeral system in mathematics&nbsp; is extremely useful, much better than&nbsp;&nbsp; the Roman numeral system, for instance. But again, there's nothing special about ten.&nbsp;

It's a system that is useful for us&nbsp; because everyone else uses it. We've&nbsp;&nbsp; standardized it. We've built all our&nbsp; computers and our number representation&nbsp;&nbsp; systems around it, so we're stuck with it now.

Some people occasionally push for other systems&nbsp;&nbsp; than decimal, but there's just too much inertia. It's not something where you can look at any given&nbsp;&nbsp; scientific achievement purely in isolation and&nbsp; give it an objective grade without being aware&nbsp;&nbsp;

of the context both in the past and the future. So it may never be something that you can&nbsp;&nbsp; just reinforcement learn the same way that&nbsp; you can for much more localized problems.&nbsp; Often in the history of science when a new theory&nbsp;

comes up that in retrospect we realize is correct,&nbsp;&nbsp; it seems to make implications that either&nbsp; make no sense because they're wrong, and we&nbsp;&nbsp; realize later on why they're wrong, or they're&nbsp; correct but seem wildly implausible at the time.&nbsp;

As you talked about, Aristarchus had&nbsp; heliocentrism in the third century BC.&nbsp; The ancient Athenians were like, "This can't be&nbsp; because if the earth is going around the sun,&nbsp;&nbsp; we should see the relative position of the stars&nbsp;

change as we're going around the sun, and the only&nbsp;&nbsp; way that wouldn't be the case is if they're so&nbsp; far away that you don't notice any parallax,"&nbsp;&nbsp; which is actually the correct implication. But there's times when the implication is&nbsp;&nbsp;

incorrect and we just need to graduate&nbsp; to a better level of understanding.&nbsp; Leibniz would chide Newton and disagree with&nbsp; Newton's theory of gravity on the basis that&nbsp;&nbsp; it implied action at a distance, and they&nbsp;

didn't know the mechanism, and Newton himself&nbsp;&nbsp; was sort of stunned that inertial mass and&nbsp; gravitational mass were the same quantity.&nbsp; All these things later were resolved by&nbsp; Einstein. But it was still progress. So&nbsp;&nbsp;

the question for a system of peer review for&nbsp; AI would be: even if you can falsify a theory,&nbsp;&nbsp; how would you notice that it still constitutes&nbsp; progress relative to the thing before?&nbsp; Often, the ultimately correct theory&nbsp;

initially is worse in many ways.&nbsp; Copernicus's theory of the planets was&nbsp; less accurate than Ptolemy's theory.&nbsp; Geocentrism had been developed for a&nbsp; millennium by that point, and they had&nbsp;&nbsp;

made many tweaks and increasingly complicated&nbsp; ad hoc fixes to make it more and more accurate.&nbsp; Copernicus's theory was a lot&nbsp; simpler but much less accurate.&nbsp; It was only Kepler that made it&nbsp;

more accurate than Ptolemy's theory.&nbsp; Science is always a work in progress. When you only get part of the solution,&nbsp;&nbsp; it looks worse than a theory which is incorrect&nbsp; but somehow has been completed to the point&nbsp;&nbsp;

where it kind of answers all the questions. As you say, Newton's theory had big mysteries.&nbsp; They had the equivalence of mass&nbsp; and action at a distance, which&nbsp;&nbsp; were only resolved with a very conceptually&nbsp;

different approach centuries afterwards.&nbsp; Often progress has to be made not by&nbsp; adding more theories, but by deleting&nbsp;&nbsp; some assumptions that you have in your mind. One reason why geocentrism held on for so long&nbsp;&nbsp;

is we had this idea that objects&nbsp; naturally want to stay at rest.&nbsp; This is the Aristotelian notion of physics,&nbsp; and so the idea that the Earth was moving…&nbsp;&nbsp; How come we weren't all falling over?

Once you have Newton's laws of motion—an&nbsp;&nbsp; object in motion remains in motion&nbsp; and so forth—then it makes sense.&nbsp; Conceptually, it's a very big leap to&nbsp; realize that the Earth is in motion.&nbsp;

It doesn't feel like it's in motion. The biggest advances, like Darwin's&nbsp;&nbsp; theory of evolution, is the idea&nbsp; that species are not static.&nbsp; This is not obvious because you&nbsp;

don't see evolution in your lifetime.&nbsp; Well, now we actually can, but&nbsp; it seems permanent and static.&nbsp; Right now we're going through a cognitive version&nbsp; of the Copernican revolution, where we used to&nbsp;&nbsp;

think that human intelligence is the center of&nbsp; the universe, and now we're seeing that there are&nbsp;&nbsp; very different types of intelligence out there&nbsp; with very different strengths and weaknesses.&nbsp; Our assessment of which tasks require&nbsp;

intelligence, which ones don't,&nbsp;&nbsp; has to be reordered quite a bit. Trying to fit AI into our theories&nbsp;&nbsp; of scientific progress and what is hard and&nbsp; what is easy, we're struggling quite a lot.&nbsp;

We have to ask questions that we've&nbsp; never really had to ask before.&nbsp; Or maybe the philosophers had, but&nbsp; now we all have to deal with it.&nbsp; This brings up a topic I've&nbsp;

been very curious about.&nbsp; You mentioned Darwin's theory of evolution. There's this book, The Clockwork Universe&nbsp;&nbsp; by Edward Dolnick, which covers a lot of&nbsp; this era of history we're talking about.&nbsp;

He has this interesting observation in there. The Origin of Species was published in 1859.&nbsp; Principia Mathematica was published in 1687. So The Origin of Species comes out two centuries&nbsp;&nbsp; after Principia.

Conceptually,&nbsp;&nbsp; it seems like Darwin's theory is simpler. There's a contemporaneous biologist to Darwin,&nbsp;&nbsp; Thomas Huxley, who reads The Origin of Species and&nbsp; he says, "How stupid not to have thought of that."&nbsp;

Nobody ever says that about&nbsp; Principia, chiding themselves&nbsp;&nbsp; for not having beaten Newton to gravity. So there's a question of why did it take longer?&nbsp; It seems like a big part of the&nbsp;

reason is what you were saying.&nbsp; The evidence for natural selection is overwhelming&nbsp; in a certain sense, but it's cumulative and&nbsp;&nbsp; retrospective, whereas Newton can&nbsp; just say, "Here are my equations.&nbsp;

Let me see the moon's orbital&nbsp; period and its distance,&nbsp;&nbsp; and if it lines up, then we've made progress." Lucretius actually had this idea that species&nbsp;&nbsp; adapted to their environment in the first&nbsp;

century BC but nobody really talks about it&nbsp;&nbsp; until Darwin because Lucretius couldn't run some&nbsp; experiment and force people to pay attention.&nbsp; I wonder if we'll in retrospect end up seeing&nbsp; much more progress in domains which have this&nbsp;&nbsp;

kind of tight data loop where you can&nbsp; verify them quite easily, even though&nbsp;&nbsp; they're conceptually much more difficult. I think one aspect of science is that it's not&nbsp;&nbsp; just creating a new theory and validating&nbsp;

it, but communicating it to others.&nbsp; Darwin was an amazing science communicator. He wrote in English, in natural language. I'm&nbsp;&nbsp; speaking like a— No Lean.&nbsp;

I have to get out of my technical mindset. He spoke in plain English, didn't use equations,&nbsp;&nbsp; and he synthesized a lot of disparate facts. Little pieces of evolution had been worked out in&nbsp;&nbsp; the past, but he had this very compelling vision.

Again, he was still missing things.&nbsp; He didn't know the mechanism for&nbsp; heredity, he didn't have DNA.&nbsp; But his writing style was persuasive, and&nbsp; that helped a lot. Newton wrote in Latin.&nbsp;&nbsp;

He had invented entire new areas of&nbsp; mathematics just to explain what he was doing.&nbsp; He was also from an era where scientists&nbsp; were much more secretive and competitive.&nbsp; Academia is still competitive, but it&nbsp;

was even worse back in Newton's day.&nbsp; He held back some of his best insights because&nbsp; he didn't want his rivals to get any advantage.&nbsp; He was also a somewhat unpleasant&nbsp; person from what I gather.&nbsp;

It was only a couple of decades after Newton&nbsp; when other scientists explained his work in&nbsp;&nbsp; much simpler terms that they became widespread. The art of exposition and making a case and&nbsp;&nbsp; creating a narrative is also a&nbsp;

very important part of science.&nbsp; If you have the data, it helps, but people need&nbsp; to be convinced, otherwise they will not push&nbsp;&nbsp; it further or take the initial investment&nbsp; to learn your theory and really explore it.&nbsp;

That's another thing which is really&nbsp; hard to reinforcement learn on.&nbsp; How can you score how persuasive you are? Well, there are entire marketing&nbsp;&nbsp; departments trying to do this.

Maybe it's good that AI is not&nbsp;&nbsp; yet optimized to be persuasive. There's a social aspect to science.&nbsp; Even though we pride ourselves on having an&nbsp; objective side to it, where there's data and&nbsp;&nbsp;

experiment and validation, we still have&nbsp; to tell stories and convince our fellow&nbsp;&nbsp; scientists. That's a soft, squishy thing. It's&nbsp; a combination of data and painting a narrative,&nbsp;&nbsp; and it's a narrative of gaps.

Even with Darwin, as I said, there&nbsp;&nbsp; were pieces of his theory he could not explain. But he could still make a case that in the future,&nbsp;&nbsp; people would find transitional&nbsp; forms, that they would find the&nbsp;&nbsp;

mechanism of inheritance, and they did. I don't know how you can quantify that&nbsp;&nbsp; in such a precise way that you can&nbsp; start doing reinforcement learning.&nbsp; Maybe that will be forever&nbsp;

the human side of science.&nbsp; One takeaway I had from reading and watching your&nbsp; stuff on the cosmic distance ladder… By the way,&nbsp;&nbsp; I highly recommend people watch your series&nbsp; with 3Blue1Brown on the cosmic distance ladder.&nbsp;

from little traces of data, almost like Sherlock. I hear that for a lot of quant hedge funds, their&nbsp;&nbsp; preferred hire is an astronomy PhD, actually. They are also very interested for other reasons&nbsp;&nbsp; in extracting signals from&nbsp;

various random bits of data.&nbsp; Okay, speaking of clever ideas,&nbsp; one of my listeners, Shawn,&nbsp;&nbsp; solved the puzzle that Jane Street made for my&nbsp; audience and posted a great walkthrough on X.&nbsp;

For context, Jane Street trained a ResNet,&nbsp; shuffled all 96 layers, and then challenged&nbsp;&nbsp; people to put them back in the right order using&nbsp; only the model's outputs and training data.&nbsp; You can't brute force this – there's more&nbsp;

possible orderings than atoms in the universe.&nbsp; So Shawn broke the problem&nbsp; into two different parts.&nbsp; First, pair the layers into 48 different blocks. And second, put those blocks in the right order.&nbsp;

For pairing, Shawn realized that in&nbsp; a well-trained ResNet, the product of&nbsp;&nbsp; two weight matrices in a residual block should&nbsp; have a distinctive negative diagonal pattern.&nbsp; This arises as a way for the model to keep the&nbsp;

residual stream from growing out of control.&nbsp; From this insight, he was able&nbsp; to recover the right pairings.&nbsp; For ordering, Shawn noticed that the model&nbsp; seemed to improve if he sorted the blocks by&nbsp;&nbsp;

the size of their residual contributions. Starting with that rough approximation,&nbsp;&nbsp; he combined a clever ranking heuristic with&nbsp; local swaps to recover the exact right order.&nbsp; His full walkthrough is linked in the description.&nbsp;

Don't worry if you didn't get&nbsp; to this puzzle in time, though.&nbsp; There's still one up about backdoored LLMs that&nbsp; even Jane Street doesn't know how to solve.&nbsp; You can find it at janestreet.com/dwarkesh.

out of the eleven hundred odd Erdős problems. I don’t know if it’s still correct, but as of&nbsp;&nbsp; a month ago you said that there had been a pause&nbsp; because the low-hanging fruit had been picked.&nbsp; First of all, I'm curious if that is still the&nbsp;

case, that we have picked the low-hanging fruit&nbsp;&nbsp; and now we're at this plateau currently. It does seem so. Fifty-odd problems have&nbsp;&nbsp; been solved with AI assistance, which is&nbsp; great, but there's like six hundred to go.&nbsp;

People are still chipping away&nbsp; at one or two of these right now.&nbsp; We're seeing a lot fewer pure AI solutions&nbsp; now where the AI just one-shots the problem.&nbsp; There was a month where that happened and&nbsp;

that has stopped, not for lack of trying.&nbsp; I know of three separate attempts to get&nbsp; frontier model AIs to just attack every&nbsp;&nbsp; single one of the problems simultaneously. They pick out some minor observations,&nbsp;&nbsp;

or maybe they find that some problem was already&nbsp; solved in the literature, but there hasn't been&nbsp;&nbsp; any further purely AI-powered solution yet. People are using AI a lot currently.&nbsp; Someone might use AI to generate a possible&nbsp;

proof strategy, and then another person will&nbsp;&nbsp; use a separate AI tool to critique it, rewrite&nbsp; it, generate some numerical data for it,&nbsp;&nbsp; or do a literature survey. Some problems have been solved&nbsp;&nbsp;

by an ongoing conversation between&nbsp; lots of humans and lots of AI tools.&nbsp; But it does seem like it was this one-off thing. Maybe one analogy for these problems is&nbsp;&nbsp; that you're in some sort of mountain&nbsp;

range with all kinds of cliffs and walls.&nbsp; Maybe there's a little wall which is three&nbsp; feet high, and one that's six feet high,&nbsp;&nbsp; and then there's fifteen feet high, and&nbsp; then there are some mile-high cliffs.&nbsp;

You're trying to climb as many of these&nbsp; cliffs as possible, but it's in the dark.&nbsp; We don't know which ones are&nbsp; tall, which ones are short.&nbsp; So we try to light some candles&nbsp;

and make some maps, and slowly we&nbsp;&nbsp; figure out some of them are climbable. Some of them we can identify a partial&nbsp;&nbsp; track in the wall that you can reach first. These AI tools, they're like jumping&nbsp;&nbsp;

machines that can jump two meters&nbsp; in the air, higher than any human.&nbsp; Sometimes they jump in the wrong&nbsp; direction, and sometimes they crash,&nbsp;&nbsp; but sometimes they can reach the tops of the&nbsp;

lowest walls that we couldn't reach before.&nbsp; We've just set them loose in this&nbsp; mountain range, hopping around.&nbsp; There was this exciting period where they could&nbsp; actually find all the low ones and reach them.&nbsp;

Maybe the next time there's a big&nbsp; advance in the models, they will&nbsp;&nbsp; try it again, and a few more will be breached. But it's a different style of doing mathematics.&nbsp; Normally we would hill climb, make little&nbsp;

markers, and try to identify partial things.&nbsp; These tools either succeed or they fail. They've been really bad at creating partial&nbsp;&nbsp; progress or identifying intermediate&nbsp; stages that you should focus on first.&nbsp;

Going back to this previous discussion, we&nbsp; don't have a way of evaluating partial progress&nbsp;&nbsp; the same way we can evaluate a one-shot&nbsp; success or failure of solving a problem.&nbsp; There's two different ways to think&nbsp;

through what you've just said.&nbsp; One of them is more bearish on AI&nbsp; progress, and one of them is more bullish.&nbsp; The bearish one being, "Oh, they're only&nbsp; getting to a certain height of wall,&nbsp;&nbsp;

which is not as high as humans are reaching." The second is that they have this powerful&nbsp;&nbsp; property that once they achieve a certain&nbsp; waterline, they can fill every single problem&nbsp;&nbsp; that is available at that waterline,&nbsp;

which we simply can't do with humans.&nbsp; We can't make a million copies of you&nbsp; and give each of them a million dollars&nbsp;&nbsp; of inference compute and have you do a hundred&nbsp; years of subjective time research on a million&nbsp;&nbsp;

different problems at the same time. But once AIs reach Terence Tao-level,&nbsp;&nbsp; they could do that. Once they reach intermediate levels,&nbsp;&nbsp; they could do the intermediate version of that.

The same reason that we should be bearish now is&nbsp;&nbsp; the reason we should be especially bullish. Not even when they achieve superhuman&nbsp;&nbsp; intelligence, but just when they&nbsp; achieve human-level intelligence,&nbsp;&nbsp;

because their human-level intelligence&nbsp; is qualitatively wider and more powerful&nbsp;&nbsp; than our human-level intelligence. I agree. They excel at breadth,&nbsp;&nbsp; and humans excel at depth, human experts at&nbsp;

least. I think they're very complementary.&nbsp;&nbsp; But our current way of doing math and science&nbsp; is focused on depth because that's where human&nbsp;&nbsp; expertise is, because humans can't do breadth. We have to redesign the way we do science to take&nbsp;&nbsp;

full advantage of this breadth&nbsp; capability that we now have.&nbsp; We should have a lot more effort in creating&nbsp; very broad classes of problems to work on rather&nbsp;&nbsp; than one or two really deep, important problems.

We should still have the deep, important problems,&nbsp;&nbsp; and humans should still be working on them. But now we have this other way of doing science.&nbsp; We can explore entirely new fields of&nbsp; science by first getting these broad,&nbsp;&nbsp;

moderately competent AIs to map it out&nbsp; and make all the easy observations.&nbsp; And then identify certain islands of difficulty,&nbsp; which human experts can then come and work on.&nbsp; I see very much a future of&nbsp;

very complementary science.&nbsp; Eventually, you would hope to get both breadth&nbsp; and depth and somehow get the best of both worlds.&nbsp; But we need practice with the breadth side.&nbsp; It's too new. We don't even have the paradigms&nbsp;&nbsp;

to really take full advantage of it. But we will, and then science will be&nbsp;&nbsp; unrecognizable after that, I think. To this point about complementarity,&nbsp;&nbsp; programmers have noticed that they're way&nbsp;

more productive as a result of these AI tools.&nbsp; I don't know if you as a mathematician&nbsp; feel the same way, but it does seem&nbsp;&nbsp; like one big difference between vibe coding&nbsp; and vibe researching is that with software,&nbsp;&nbsp;

the whole point is to have some&nbsp; effect on the world through your work.&nbsp; If it leads to you better understanding&nbsp; a problem or coming up with some clean&nbsp;&nbsp; abstraction to embody in your code,&nbsp;

that is instrumental to the end goal.&nbsp; Whereas with research, the reason we care&nbsp; about solving the Millennium Prize Problems&nbsp;&nbsp; is that presumably that in the process of&nbsp; solving them, we discover new mathematical&nbsp;&nbsp;

objects or new techniques that advance our&nbsp; civilization's understanding of mathematics.&nbsp; So the proof is instrumental&nbsp; to the intermediate work.&nbsp; I don't know if you agree with that dichotomy&nbsp;

or if that in any way will explain the relative&nbsp;&nbsp; uplift we'll see in software versus research. Certainly in math, the process is often more&nbsp;&nbsp; important than the problem itself. The problem is kind of a proxy&nbsp;&nbsp;

for measuring progress. I think even in software,&nbsp;&nbsp; there are different types of software tasks. If you just create a webpage that does the same&nbsp;&nbsp; thing that a thousand other webpages&nbsp;

do, there's no skill to be learned.&nbsp; Well, there is still some skill maybe that&nbsp; the individual programmer could pick up.&nbsp; But for boilerplate-type code, it's something&nbsp; that you should definitely offload to AI.&nbsp;

Sometimes once you make the code,&nbsp; you still have to maintain it.&nbsp; There are issues with upgrading it and&nbsp; making it compatible with other things.&nbsp; I've heard programmers report that even&nbsp;

if an AI can create the first prototype&nbsp;&nbsp; of a tool, making it mesh with everything&nbsp; else and making it interact with the real&nbsp;&nbsp; world in the way they want is an ongoing process. If you don't have the skills that you pick up from&nbsp;&nbsp;

writing the code, that may impact your&nbsp; ability to maintain it down the road.&nbsp; So yes, certainly mathematicians, we've used&nbsp; problems to build intuition and to train people&nbsp;&nbsp; to have a good idea of what's true, what to&nbsp;

expect, what is provable, and what is difficult.&nbsp; Just getting the answers right away&nbsp; may actually inhibit that process.&nbsp; I made a distinction between&nbsp; theory and experiment before.&nbsp;

In most sciences, there's an equal&nbsp; division between the theoretical side&nbsp;&nbsp; and the experimental side. Math has been unique in&nbsp;&nbsp; that it's almost entirely theoretical.

We place a premium on trying to have coherent,&nbsp;&nbsp; clean theories of why things are true and false. We haven't done many experiments as to,&nbsp;&nbsp; if we have two different ways to solve&nbsp; a problem, which is more effective.&nbsp;

We have some intuition, but we haven't done&nbsp; large-scale studies where we take a thousand&nbsp;&nbsp; problems and just test them. But we can do that now.&nbsp; I think AI-type tools will actually&nbsp;

revolutionize the experimental side of math,&nbsp;&nbsp; where you don't care so much about individual&nbsp; problems and the process of solving them,&nbsp;&nbsp; but you want to gather large-scale data&nbsp; about what things work and what things don't.&nbsp;

The same way that if you're a software&nbsp; company and you want to roll out a thousand&nbsp;&nbsp; pieces of software, you don't really want to&nbsp; handcraft each one and learn lessons from each.&nbsp; You just want to find what&nbsp;

workflows let you scale.&nbsp; The idea of doing mathematics&nbsp; at scale is at its infancy.&nbsp; But that's where AI is really&nbsp; going to revolutionize the subject.&nbsp;

I feel like a big crux in these conversations&nbsp; about how good AI will be for science is,&nbsp;&nbsp; I think you said this, that they're using&nbsp; existing techniques and modifying them.&nbsp; It would be interesting to&nbsp;

understand how much progress one&nbsp;&nbsp; can make simply from using existing techniques. If I looked at the top math journals, how many of&nbsp;&nbsp; the papers are coming up with a new technique,&nbsp; whatever that means, versus using existing&nbsp;&nbsp;

techniques on new problems? What is the overhang?&nbsp; If you just applied every known technique to every&nbsp;&nbsp; open problem, would that constitute a humongous&nbsp; uplift in our civilization's knowledge, or would&nbsp;&nbsp; that not be that impressive and useful?

This is a great question, and we don't&nbsp;&nbsp; have the data to fully answer it yet. Certainly, a lot of work that human&nbsp;&nbsp; mathematicians do… When you take a new problem,&nbsp; one of the first things we do is we look at all&nbsp;&nbsp;

the standard things that have worked on similar&nbsp; problems in the past, and we try them one by one.&nbsp; Sometimes that works, and that's still worth&nbsp; publishing because the question was important.&nbsp; Sometimes they almost work,&nbsp;

and you have to add one more&nbsp;&nbsp; wrinkle to it, and that's also interesting. But the papers that go into the top journals&nbsp;&nbsp; are usually ones where the existing methods&nbsp; can kind of solve 80% of the problem, but then&nbsp;&nbsp;

there is this 20% which is resistant and a new&nbsp; technique has to be invented to fill in the gaps.&nbsp; It's very rare now that a problem gets&nbsp; solved with no reliance on past literature,&nbsp;&nbsp; where all the ideas come out of nowhere.

That was more common in the past,&nbsp;&nbsp; but math is so mature now that it's just so much&nbsp; of a handicap to not use the literature first.&nbsp; AI tools are getting really good at the&nbsp; first part of that, just trying all the&nbsp;&nbsp;

standard techniques on a problem, often making&nbsp; fewer mistakes in applying them than humans.&nbsp; They still make mistakes, but I've tested&nbsp; these tools on little tasks that I can do,&nbsp;&nbsp; and sometimes they pick up errors that I make.

Sometimes I pick up errors that they make.&nbsp; It's about a tie right now. But I haven't yet seen them take the next step.&nbsp; When there are holes in the argument where none&nbsp; of the things are working, then what do you do?&nbsp;

They can suggest random things, but often&nbsp; I find that trying to chase them down to&nbsp;&nbsp; make them work, and finding they don't&nbsp; work, wastes more time than it saves.&nbsp; I think some fraction of problems that&nbsp;

we currently think are hard will fall&nbsp;&nbsp; from this method, especially the ones&nbsp; that haven't received enough attention.&nbsp; With the Erdős problems, almost all of the 50&nbsp; problems that were solved by AIs were ones for&nbsp;&nbsp;

which there was basically no literature. Erdős posed the problem once or twice.&nbsp; Maybe some people tried it casually and couldn't&nbsp; do it, but they never wrote up anything.&nbsp; But it turned out that there was a solution,&nbsp;

and it was just combining this one obscure&nbsp;&nbsp; technique that not many people know about&nbsp; with some other result in the literature.&nbsp; That's the median level of what AI can&nbsp; accomplish, and that's really great.&nbsp;

It clears out 50 of these problems. So I think you will see some isolated successes.&nbsp; But what we found… Some people have done&nbsp; large-scale sweeps of these Erdős problems.&nbsp; If you only focus on the success&nbsp;

stories, the ones that get broadcast&nbsp;&nbsp; on social media, it looks amazing. All these problems that haven't been&nbsp;&nbsp; solved for decades, now they're falling. But whenever we do a systematic study,&nbsp;&nbsp;

on any given problem an AI tool has&nbsp; a success rate of maybe 1% or 2%.&nbsp; It's just that they can buy scale, and you&nbsp; just pick the winners. It looks great. I&nbsp;&nbsp; think there'll be a similar thing happening&nbsp;

with the hundreds of really prestigious,&nbsp;&nbsp; difficult math problems out there. Some AI may get lucky and actually solve them,&nbsp;&nbsp; and there will be some backdoor to solve&nbsp; the problem that everyone else missed.&nbsp;

That will get a lot of publicity. But then people will try these fancy&nbsp;&nbsp; tools on their own favorite problem, and they&nbsp; will again experience the 1% to 2% success rate.&nbsp; There'll be a lot of noise amongst the signal&nbsp;

of when they're working and when they're not.&nbsp; It will be increasingly important to&nbsp; collect these really standardized datasets.&nbsp; There are efforts now to create a standard set of&nbsp; challenge problems for AIs to solve, and not just&nbsp;&nbsp;

rely on the AI companies to only publish their&nbsp; wins and not disclose their negative results.&nbsp; That will maybe give more clarity&nbsp; as to where we're actually at.&nbsp; Although I think it's worth emphasizing how&nbsp;

much progress in AI it constitutes already,&nbsp;&nbsp; to have models that are capable of applying&nbsp; some technique that nobody had written down&nbsp;&nbsp; as applicable to this particular problem. The progress is simultaneously amazing&nbsp;&nbsp;

and disappointing. It is a very strange&nbsp;&nbsp; feeling to see these tools in action. But people also acclimatize really quickly.&nbsp; I remember when Google's web&nbsp;

search came out 20 years ago.&nbsp; It just blew all the other&nbsp; searches out of the water.&nbsp; You're getting relevant hits on the&nbsp; front page, exactly what you wanted.&nbsp;

It was amazing, and then after&nbsp; a few years, you just took for&nbsp;&nbsp; granted that you could Google anything. 2026-level AI would be stunning in 2021.&nbsp; A lot of it—face recognition, natural speech,&nbsp;

doing college-level math problems—we just&nbsp;&nbsp; take for granted now. Speaking of 2026 AI,&nbsp;&nbsp; you made a prediction in 2023 that by 2026&nbsp; it would be like a colleague in mathematics?&nbsp;

A trustworthy co-author if used correctly. Which is looking pretty good in retrospect.&nbsp; Yeah, I'm pretty pleased. So let's see if you can continue this streak.&nbsp; You personally are 2x more&nbsp;

productive as a result of AI.&nbsp; What year would you say that? Productivity, I think,&nbsp;&nbsp; is not quite a one-dimensional quantity. I'm definitely noticing that the style&nbsp;&nbsp;

in which I do mathematics is changing&nbsp; quite a bit, and the type of things I do.&nbsp; For example, my papers now have a&nbsp; lot more code, a lot more pictures,&nbsp;&nbsp; because it's so easy to generate these things now.

Some plot which would have taken me hours to do,&nbsp;&nbsp; now I can do in minutes. But in the past, I just wouldn't have&nbsp;&nbsp; put the plot in my paper in the first place. I would just talk about it in words.&nbsp;

So it's hard to measure what 2x means. On the one hand, I think the type of&nbsp;&nbsp; papers that I would write today, if I&nbsp; had to do them without AI assistance,&nbsp;&nbsp; would definitely take five times longer.

But I would not write my papers that way.&nbsp; 5x? Yeah, but these are auxiliary tasks.&nbsp; Things like doing a much deeper literature&nbsp; search or supplying a lot more numerics.&nbsp;&nbsp;

They enrich the paper. The core of what I do,&nbsp; actually solving the most difficult part of a&nbsp;&nbsp; math problem, hasn't changed too much. I still use pen and paper for that.&nbsp; But there's lots of silly things.

I use an AI agent now to reformat.&nbsp; Sometimes if all my parentheses are not quite&nbsp; the right size, I used to manually change them&nbsp;&nbsp; by hand, and now I can get an AI agent to&nbsp; do all that quite nicely in the background.&nbsp;

They've really sped up lots of secondary tasks. They haven't yet sped up the core thing that I do,&nbsp;&nbsp; but it's allowed me to add&nbsp; more things to my papers.&nbsp; By the same token, if I were to write a paper&nbsp;

I wrote in 2020 again—and not add all these&nbsp;&nbsp; extra features, but just have something of&nbsp; the same level of functionality—it actually&nbsp;&nbsp; hasn't saved that much time, to be honest. It's made the papers richer and broader,&nbsp;&nbsp;

but not necessarily deeper. You made this distinction between&nbsp;&nbsp; artificial cleverness and artificial intelligence. I would like to better understand those concepts.&nbsp; What is an example of intelligence&nbsp;

that is not just cleverness?&nbsp; Intelligence is famously hard to define.&nbsp; It's one of these things that&nbsp; you know when you see it.&nbsp; But when I talk to someone and we're trying to&nbsp;

collaboratively solve a math problem together,&nbsp;&nbsp; there's this conversation where neither of&nbsp; us knows how to solve the problem initially.&nbsp; One of us has some idea and it looks promising,&nbsp; so then we have some sort of prototype strategy.&nbsp;

We test it, and it doesn't&nbsp; work, but then we modify it.&nbsp; There's adaptivity and continual&nbsp; improvement of the idea over time.&nbsp; Eventually, we've systematically mapped&nbsp;

out what doesn't work and what does work,&nbsp;&nbsp; and we can see a path forward, but&nbsp; it's evolving with our discussion.&nbsp; This isn't quite what the AIs do. The AIs can mimic this a little bit.&nbsp;

To go back to this analogy of these jumping&nbsp; robots, they can jump and fail, and jump and fail.&nbsp; But what they can't do is jump a little bit, reach&nbsp; some handhold, stay there, pull other people up,&nbsp;&nbsp; and then try to jump from there.

There isn't this cumulative process&nbsp;&nbsp; which is built up interactively. It seems to be a lot more trial and&nbsp;&nbsp; error and just repetition: brute force. It scales, and it can work amazingly&nbsp;&nbsp;

well in certain contexts. But this idea of building&nbsp;&nbsp; up cumulatively from partial progress&nbsp; is what's still not quite there yet.&nbsp; Interesting. You're saying if Gemini 3 or&nbsp;

Claude 4.5, whatever, solves a problem,&nbsp;&nbsp; it is not the case that its own&nbsp; understanding of math has progressed.&nbsp; No. Or even if it works&nbsp;&nbsp;

on a problem without solving it, it's not that&nbsp; its own understanding of math has progressed.&nbsp; Yeah. You run a new session and&nbsp; it's forgotten what it just did.&nbsp; It has no new skills to build on related problems.

Maybe what you just did is 0.001% of the&nbsp;&nbsp; training data for the next generation. So maybe eventually some of it gets absorbed.&nbsp; So Terence talks about the importance&nbsp; of decomposing particularly gnarly&nbsp;&nbsp;

problems into a series of easier chunks. Even if this doesn't result in the full solution,&nbsp;&nbsp; approaching problems in this way helps you build&nbsp; up the intuitions and practice the techniques&nbsp;&nbsp; that you'll need to keep making progress.

But models today tend to struggle with these&nbsp;&nbsp; kinds of problem-solving techniques. That's where Labelbox comes in.&nbsp; Labelbox helps you train models not just to get&nbsp; the right answer, but to think the right way.&nbsp;

They've operationalized these reasoning behaviors&nbsp; into rubrics, giving you the ability to evaluate&nbsp;&nbsp; every important dimension of a model's output. These rubrics go beyond simple correctness.&nbsp; Did the model reach for the right tools?

Did it check its own work and&nbsp;&nbsp; explore alternative paths? How clear was its response?&nbsp; These skills are useful across domains:&nbsp; math, physics, finance, psychology, and more.&nbsp;

And they're becoming increasingly important&nbsp; as models take on harder, open-ended problems,&nbsp;&nbsp; some of which have multiple solutions and some&nbsp; of which we don't even know the solutions to.&nbsp; Labelbox can get you rubrics tailored to&nbsp;

your domain, helping you systematically&nbsp;&nbsp; measure and shape how your models think. Learn more at labelbox.com/dwarkesh.&nbsp; One big question I have is how plausible is it&nbsp; that if we just keep training AIs—they get better&nbsp;&nbsp;

and better at solving problems in Lean—that they&nbsp; will continue to solve more and more impressive&nbsp;&nbsp; problems, and then we will be surprised at how&nbsp; little insight we got from some Lean solution&nbsp;&nbsp; to proving the Riemann hypothesis or something.

Or do you think it is a necessary condition of&nbsp;&nbsp; solving the Riemann hypothesis, even by&nbsp; an AI that is doing it entirely in Lean,&nbsp;&nbsp; that the constructions and definitions&nbsp; created in the Lean program have to&nbsp;&nbsp;

advance our understanding of mathematics? Or could it just be assembly code gobbledygook?&nbsp; We don't know. Some problems have been&nbsp; basically solved by pure brute force.&nbsp; The four color theorem is a famous example.

We have still not found a conceptually elegant&nbsp;&nbsp; proof of this theorem, and maybe we never will. Some problems may only be solvable by splitting&nbsp;&nbsp; into an enormous number of&nbsp; cases and doing brute force,&nbsp;&nbsp;

uninsightful computer analysis on each case. Part of the reason we prize problems like&nbsp;&nbsp; the Riemann hypothesis is that we're&nbsp; pretty sure a new type of mathematics&nbsp;&nbsp; has to be created, or a new connection between&nbsp;

two previously unconnected areas of mathematics&nbsp;&nbsp; has to be discovered to make this work. We don't even know what the shape of the solution&nbsp;&nbsp; is, but it doesn't feel like a problem that will&nbsp; be solved just by exhaustively checking cases.&nbsp;

Or it could be false actually. Okay, there is an unlikely scenario&nbsp;&nbsp; that the hypothesis is false, and you&nbsp; can just compute a zero off the line,&nbsp;&nbsp; and a massive computer calculation verifies&nbsp;

it. That would be very disappointing. I do&nbsp;&nbsp; feel that fully autonomous, one-shot approaches&nbsp; are not the right approach for these problems.&nbsp; You'll get a lot more mileage out of the interplay&nbsp; of humans collaborating with these tools.&nbsp;

I can see one of these problems&nbsp; being solved by smart humans&nbsp;&nbsp; assisted by extremely powerful AI tools. But the exact dynamic may be very different&nbsp;&nbsp; from what we envision right now.

It could be a collaboration of&nbsp;&nbsp; a type that just doesn't exist yet. There may be a way to generate a million variants&nbsp;&nbsp; of the Riemann zeta function and do AI-assisted&nbsp; data analysis to discover some pattern connecting&nbsp;&nbsp;

them that we didn't know about before. This lets you transform the problem&nbsp;&nbsp; into a different area of mathematics. There could be all kinds of scenarios.&nbsp; Suppose the AI figures it out, and latent in&nbsp;

the Lean is some brand-new construction which,&nbsp;&nbsp; if we realized its significance, we would be&nbsp; able to apply in all these different situations.&nbsp; How would we even recognize it? Again, a very naive question, but if you come&nbsp;&nbsp;

up with the equivalent of Descartes' idea that&nbsp; you can have a coordinate system unifying algebra&nbsp;&nbsp; and geometry, in Lean code it would just look&nbsp; like R→R, and it wouldn't look that significant.&nbsp; I'm sure there are other constructions&nbsp;

which have this kind of property.&nbsp; The beauty of formalizing a proof in&nbsp; something like Lean is that you can take&nbsp;&nbsp; any piece of it and study it atomically. When I read a paper which solves some&nbsp;&nbsp;

difficult problem, there's often a&nbsp; big sequence of lemmas and theorems.&nbsp; Ideally, the author will talk their way&nbsp; through what's important and what's not.&nbsp; But sometimes they don't reveal what steps&nbsp;

were the important ones and which ones&nbsp;&nbsp; were just boilerplate, standard steps. You can study each lemma in isolation.&nbsp; Some of them I can see look fairly standard&nbsp; and resemble something I'm familiar with.&nbsp;

I'm pretty sure there's nothing&nbsp; interesting going on there.&nbsp; But this other lemma, that's something I haven't&nbsp; seen before, and I can see why having this result&nbsp;&nbsp; would really help prove the main result.

You can assess whether a step is really key&nbsp;&nbsp; to your argument or not, and&nbsp; Lean really facilitates that.&nbsp; The individual steps are&nbsp; identified really precisely.&nbsp;

I think in the future, there will be entire&nbsp; professions of mathematicians who might take&nbsp;&nbsp; a giant Lean-generated proof and do some&nbsp; ablation on it, trying to remove parts of&nbsp;&nbsp; it and find more elegant ways.

They might get other AIs to do&nbsp;&nbsp; some reinforcement learning to make the proof&nbsp; more elegant, and maybe other AIs will grade&nbsp;&nbsp; whether this proof looks better or not. One thing that will change quite a bit&nbsp;&nbsp;

in the near future is how we write papers. Until recently, writing papers was the most&nbsp;&nbsp; time-consuming and expensive part of the job. So you did it very rarely.&nbsp; You only wrote up your results once all the other&nbsp;

parts of your argument were checked out, because&nbsp;&nbsp; rewriting and refactoring was just a total pain. That's become a lot easier now&nbsp;&nbsp; with modern AI tools. You don't have to have just&nbsp;&nbsp;

one version of your paper. Once you have one,&nbsp;&nbsp; people can generate hundreds more. One giant messy Lean proof may not be very&nbsp;&nbsp; meaningful or understandable on&nbsp;

its own, but other people can&nbsp;&nbsp; refactor it and do all kinds of things with it. We've seen this with the Erdős problem website.&nbsp; An AI will generate a proof, and here are&nbsp; 3,000 lines of code that verify the proof.&nbsp;

Then people got other AIs to summarize&nbsp; the proof, and people write their own&nbsp;&nbsp; proofs. There's actually post-processing.&nbsp; Once you have one proof, we have a lot of&nbsp;&nbsp; tools now to deconstruct and interpret it.

It's a very nascent area of mathematics,&nbsp;&nbsp; but I'm not as worried about it. Some people are concerned about what happens if&nbsp;&nbsp; the Riemann hypothesis is proven with&nbsp; a completely incomprehensible proof.&nbsp;

I think once you have the artifact of a&nbsp; proof, we can do a lot of analysis on it.&nbsp; You posted recently that it would be&nbsp; helpful to have a formal or semi-formal&nbsp;&nbsp; language for mathematical strategies&nbsp;

as opposed to just mathematical proofs,&nbsp;&nbsp; which is what Lean specializes in. I would love to learn more about&nbsp;&nbsp; what that would involve or look like. We don't really know. We've been very&nbsp;&nbsp;

lucky in mathematics that we have worked&nbsp; out the laws of logic and mathematics,&nbsp;&nbsp; but this is a fairly recent accomplishment. It was started by Euclid two millennia ago,&nbsp;&nbsp; but only in the early 20th century did we&nbsp;

finally list out the axioms of mathematics,&nbsp;&nbsp; the standard axioms of what we call ZFC, the&nbsp; axioms of first-order logic, and what a proof is.&nbsp; This we've managed to automate&nbsp; and have a formal language for.&nbsp;

There could be some way to assess plausibility. You have a conjecture that something is true,&nbsp;&nbsp; you test a few examples, and it works out. How does this increase your&nbsp;&nbsp; confidence that the conjecture is true?

We have a few sort of mathematical ways to model&nbsp;&nbsp; this, like Bayesian probability, for example. But you often have to set certain base&nbsp;&nbsp; assumptions, and there's a lot of&nbsp; subjectivity still in these tasks.&nbsp;

This is more of a wish than a plan to develop&nbsp; these languages, but just seeing how successful&nbsp;&nbsp; having a formal framework in place, like Lean, has&nbsp; made deductive proofs so much easier to automate&nbsp;&nbsp; and train AI on… The bottleneck for using AI to&nbsp;

create strategies and make conjectures is we have&nbsp;&nbsp; to rely on human experts and the test of time to&nbsp; validate whether something is plausible or not.&nbsp; If there was some semi-formal framework&nbsp; where this could be done semi-automatically&nbsp;&nbsp;

in a way that isn't easily hackable... It's really important with these formal&nbsp;&nbsp; proof assistants that there are no backdoors&nbsp; or exploits you can use to somehow get your&nbsp;&nbsp; certified proof without actually proving&nbsp;

it, because reinforcement learning is&nbsp;&nbsp; just so good at finding these backdoors. If there's some framework that mimics how&nbsp;&nbsp; scientists talk to each other in a&nbsp; semi-formal way, using data and argument,&nbsp;&nbsp;

but also constructing narratives... There's some subjective aspect of&nbsp;&nbsp; science that we don't know how to capture in a way&nbsp; that we can insert AI into it in any useful way.&nbsp;&nbsp; This is a future problem. There are research&nbsp;

efforts to try to create automated conjectures,&nbsp;&nbsp; and maybe there are ways to benchmark these and&nbsp; simulate this, but it's all very new science.&nbsp; Can you help me get some intuition? I have two&nbsp; sub-questions. One, it would be very helpful&nbsp;&nbsp;

to have a specific example of what something&nbsp; like this would look like, the way scientists&nbsp;&nbsp; communicate that we can't formalize yet. Two, it seems almost definitionally paradoxical&nbsp;&nbsp; to say you're building up some narrative or&nbsp;

natural language explanation and then also having&nbsp;&nbsp; something which you could have formalized. I'm sure there's some intuition behind&nbsp;&nbsp; where that overlap is, and I'd&nbsp; love to understand that better.&nbsp;

An example of a conjecture: Gauss was&nbsp; interested in the prime numbers and&nbsp;&nbsp; created one of the first mathematical datasets. He just computed the first 100,000 prime numbers&nbsp;&nbsp; or so, hoping to find patterns.

He did find a pattern,&nbsp;&nbsp; but maybe not the pattern he was expecting. He found a statistical pattern in the primes&nbsp;&nbsp; that if you count how many primes there are&nbsp; up to 100, 1,000, one million, and so forth,&nbsp;&nbsp;

they get sparser and sparser, but the drop-off&nbsp; in the density was inversely proportional to&nbsp;&nbsp; the natural logarithm of the range of numbers. So he conjectured what we now call the prime&nbsp;&nbsp; number theorem: the number of primes up&nbsp;

to X is X divided by the natural log of X.&nbsp; He had no way to prove this. It was&nbsp; data-driven. This was a conjecture.&nbsp;&nbsp; It was revolutionary for its time because it&nbsp; was maybe the first really important conjecture&nbsp;&nbsp;

of math that was statistical in nature. Normally you're talking about a pattern,&nbsp;&nbsp; like maybe the spacing between the&nbsp; primes has a certain regularity.&nbsp; But this didn't tell you exactly how many&nbsp;

primes there were in any given range.&nbsp; It just gave you an approximation that got better&nbsp; and better as you went further and further out.&nbsp; It started the field of what&nbsp; we call analytic number theory.&nbsp;

It was the first in many conjectures&nbsp; like this, many of which got proved,&nbsp;&nbsp; which started consolidating the idea that the&nbsp; prime numbers didn't really have a pattern,&nbsp;&nbsp; that they behaved like random sets&nbsp;

of numbers with a certain density.&nbsp; They had some patterns,&nbsp; like they're almost all odd.&nbsp; They're also not actually random,&nbsp; they're what's called pseudo-random.&nbsp;

There's no random number generation&nbsp; involved in creating the prime numbers.&nbsp; But over time, it became more and more&nbsp; productive to think of the primes as&nbsp;&nbsp; if they were just generated by some god rolling&nbsp;

dice all the time and creating this random set.&nbsp; This allowed us to make all&nbsp; these other predictions.&nbsp; There's a still-open conjecture in number&nbsp; theory called the twin prime conjecture, that&nbsp;&nbsp;

there should be infinitely many pairs of primes&nbsp; that are twins just two apart, like 11 and 13.&nbsp; We can't prove that, and there are&nbsp; good reasons why we can't prove it.&nbsp; But because of this statistical random model of&nbsp;

the primes, we are absolutely convinced it's true.&nbsp; We know that if the primes were generated by&nbsp; flipping coins, we would just—by random chance&nbsp;&nbsp; like infinite monkeys at a typewriter—see&nbsp; twin primes appear over and over again.&nbsp;

We have over time developed this very accurate&nbsp; conceptual model of what the primes should behave&nbsp;&nbsp; like based on statistics and probability. It's mostly heuristic and non-rigorous,&nbsp;&nbsp; but extremely accurate.

The few times when we actually&nbsp;&nbsp; can prove things about the primes, it has&nbsp; matched up with the predictions of what we&nbsp;&nbsp; call the random model of the primes. We have this conjectural concept&nbsp;&nbsp;

framework for understanding the&nbsp; primes that everyone believes in.&nbsp; It's the same reason why we believe the&nbsp; Riemann hypothesis is true, and why we&nbsp;&nbsp; believe that cryptography based on&nbsp;

the primes is mathematically secure.&nbsp; It's all part of this belief. In fact, one reason why we care&nbsp;&nbsp; about the Riemann hypothesis is that&nbsp; if the Riemann hypothesis failed,&nbsp;&nbsp;

if we knew it was false, it would&nbsp; be a serious blow to this model.&nbsp; It would mean there's a secret pattern&nbsp; to the primes that we were not aware of.&nbsp; I think we would very rapidly abandon&nbsp;

any cryptography based on the primes,&nbsp;&nbsp; because if there was one pattern that we didn't&nbsp; know about, there are probably more, and these&nbsp;&nbsp; patterns can lead to exploits in crypto. It would be a big shock.&nbsp;

So we really want to make&nbsp; sure that doesn't happen.&nbsp; We've been convinced of things like&nbsp; the Riemann hypothesis over time.&nbsp; Some of it is experimental evidence, and some&nbsp;

is that the few times we've been able to make&nbsp;&nbsp; theoretical results, they've always aligned. It is possible that the consensus is wrong and&nbsp;&nbsp; we've all just missed something very basic. There have been paradigm shifts in&nbsp;&nbsp;

the past in scientific history. But we don't really have a way of&nbsp;&nbsp; measuring this, partly because we don't have&nbsp; enough data on how math or science develops.&nbsp; We have one timeline of history, and we have&nbsp;

maybe 100 stories of turning points in history.&nbsp; If we had access to a million alien&nbsp; civilizations, each with a different&nbsp;&nbsp; development of history and science in different&nbsp; orders, then maybe we'd actually have a decent&nbsp;&nbsp;

shot at understanding how we measure what&nbsp; progress is and what is a good strategy.&nbsp; We could maybe start formalizing&nbsp; it and actually having a framework.&nbsp; Maybe what we need to do is start creating&nbsp;

lots of mini-universes or simulations of AI&nbsp;&nbsp; solving very basic problems in arithmetic&nbsp; or whatever, but coming up with their&nbsp;&nbsp; own strategies for doing these things and&nbsp; having these little laboratories to test.&nbsp;

There are people who investigate what's&nbsp; the smallest neural network that can do&nbsp;&nbsp; 10-digit multiplication and things like that. I think we could learn a lot just from evolving&nbsp;&nbsp; small AIs on simple problems.

Humans also, I think it was Berlin who&nbsp;&nbsp; split them into hedgehogs and foxes. The hedgehog knows one thing very well,&nbsp;&nbsp; and a fox knows a little bit about everything. I definitely think of myself as a fox.&nbsp;

I work with hedgehogs a lot, and&nbsp; sometimes I can be a hedgehog if need be.&nbsp; I've always had a little&nbsp; bit of an obsessive streak.&nbsp; If there's something I read about which I&nbsp;

feel like I have the capability to understand,&nbsp;&nbsp; but I don't understand why it works and&nbsp; there's some magic in it… Someone was able&nbsp;&nbsp; to use a type of mathematics I'm not familiar&nbsp; with and get a result I would like to prove.&nbsp;

I can't do it myself, but they&nbsp; could do it by their method,&nbsp;&nbsp; and I want to find out what their trick was. It bugs me that someone else can do something&nbsp;&nbsp; I think I can do, but I can't.

and say, "Okay, I'm going to remember this."&nbsp; Then six months later, I'd forgotten it. I remember remembering it,&nbsp;&nbsp; but I can't reconstruct my arguments. The first few times, it was so frustrating&nbsp;&nbsp;

Maybe there's a danger in modern&nbsp; societies, not just with AI, that we've&nbsp;&nbsp; become really good at optimizing everything. We’re not optimizing our own optimization.&nbsp; With COVID, for example, we switched a lot to&nbsp;

the library to look for a journal article.&nbsp; You had to physically check out&nbsp; the journal and read the article.&nbsp; You could browse through and sometimes&nbsp; the next article was also interesting.&nbsp;

Sometimes it wasn’t, but you could&nbsp; accidentally find interesting things.&nbsp; That has basically been lost now. If you want to access an article,&nbsp;&nbsp; you just type it into a search engine or an AI,&nbsp;

and you get exactly what you want instantly.&nbsp; But you don't get the accidental things you might&nbsp; have found if you'd done it more inefficiently.&nbsp; I spent a year once at the Institute&nbsp; for Advanced Study, which is&nbsp;&nbsp;

a great place with no distractions. You're there just to do research.&nbsp; The first few weeks you're there, it's great. You're getting all these papers written up that&nbsp;&nbsp; you've been wanting to do for a long time.

You think about problems for&nbsp;&nbsp; blocks of hours at a time. But I find if I stay there for more&nbsp;&nbsp; than several months, I run out of inspiration.&nbsp; I get bored. I surf the internet a lot more.&nbsp;

You actually do need a certain&nbsp; level of distraction in your life.&nbsp; It adds enough randomness and high temperature. I don't know the optimal way to schedule&nbsp;&nbsp; my life. It just seems to work.

I'm very curious when you expect AIs&nbsp;&nbsp; that can actually do frontier math at least&nbsp; as well as the best human mathematicians.&nbsp; In some ways, they're already doing frontier math&nbsp; that is super intelligent that humans can't do,&nbsp;&nbsp;

but it's a different frontier&nbsp; from what we're used to.&nbsp; You could argue that calculators were doing&nbsp; frontier math that humans could not accomplish,&nbsp;&nbsp; but it was number crunching.

But replacing Terry Tao completely.&nbsp; I mean, what do you want me for? You'll just go on all the podcasts after.&nbsp; It might not be the right question to ask. I think within a decade, a lot of things that&nbsp;&nbsp;

math students currently do—what we spend the&nbsp; bulk of our time doing and a lot of stuff we&nbsp;&nbsp; put in our papers today—can be done by AI. But we will find that that actually wasn't&nbsp;&nbsp; the most important part of what we do.

A hundred years ago, a lot of mathematicians&nbsp;&nbsp; were just solving differential equations. Physicists needed some exact solution to&nbsp;&nbsp; some system, and they hired a mathematician to&nbsp; laboriously go through the calculus and work out&nbsp;&nbsp;

the solution to this fluid equation, whatever. A lot of what a 19th-century mathematician would&nbsp;&nbsp; do, you could make a call to Mathematica, Wolfram&nbsp; Alpha, a computer algebra package, or now more&nbsp;&nbsp; recently to an AI, and it would just solve the&nbsp;

problem in a few minutes. But we moved on. We&nbsp;&nbsp; worked on different types of problems after that. Once computers came along—computers&nbsp;&nbsp; used to be human. People used to laboriously&nbsp;&nbsp;

create log tables and work out primes as&nbsp; Gauss did, and that has all been outsourced&nbsp;&nbsp; to computers. But we moved on. In genetics,&nbsp; to sequence the genome of a single organism,&nbsp;&nbsp; that was an entire PhD of a geneticist, carefully&nbsp;

separating all the chromosomes and whatever.&nbsp; Now you can just spend $1,000 and send&nbsp; it to a sequencer and get it done.&nbsp; But genetics is not dead as a subject. You move to a different scale.&nbsp;

Maybe you study whole ecosystems&nbsp; rather than individuals.&nbsp; I take your point but when is most&nbsp; mathematical progress, or almost&nbsp;&nbsp; all mathematical progress, happening by AI?

If you find out this year a Millennium Prize&nbsp;&nbsp; Problem has been solved, you would put&nbsp; 95% odds that an AI did it autonomously.&nbsp; Surely there will be such a year. I guess I do believe that hybrid&nbsp;&nbsp;

human plus AIs will dominate mathematics for&nbsp; a lot longer. It will depend. It will require&nbsp;&nbsp; some additional breakthroughs beyond what we&nbsp; already have, so it's going to be stochastic.&nbsp; I think AIs currently are very good at&nbsp;

certain things, but really terrible at others.&nbsp; While you can add more and more frameworks on top&nbsp; to reduce the error rates and make them work with&nbsp;&nbsp; each other a bit more, it feels like we don't&nbsp; have all the ingredients to really have a truly&nbsp;&nbsp;

satisfactory replacement for all intellectual&nbsp; tasks. It is complementary currently. It's not&nbsp;&nbsp; a replacement. Because current level AIs&nbsp; will accelerate science in so many ways,&nbsp;&nbsp; hopefully new discoveries and new&nbsp;

breakthroughs will happen more quickly.&nbsp; It's also possible that by destroying serendipity&nbsp; we actually inhibit certain types of progress.&nbsp; Anything is possible at this point. I think the world is very,&nbsp;&nbsp;

very unpredictable at this point in time. What is your advice to somebody who would&nbsp;&nbsp; consider a career in math or is early in a career&nbsp; in math, especially in light of AI progress?&nbsp; How should they be thinking about&nbsp;

their career differently, if at all,&nbsp;&nbsp; as a result of AI progress? We live in a time of change.&nbsp; As I said, we live in a&nbsp; particularly unpredictable era.&nbsp;

Things that we've taken for granted&nbsp; for centuries may not hold anymore.&nbsp; The way we do everything, and not&nbsp; just mathematics, will change.&nbsp; In many ways, I would prefer the much more&nbsp;

boring, quiet era where things are much the&nbsp;&nbsp; same as they were 10 years ago, 20 years ago. But I think one just has to embrace that&nbsp;&nbsp; there's going to be a lot of change. The things that you study, some of them&nbsp;&nbsp;

may become obsolete or revolutionized,&nbsp; but some things will be retained.&nbsp; You always have to keep an eye on opportunities&nbsp; for things that you wouldn't be able to do before.&nbsp; In math, you previously had to go through&nbsp;

years and years of education and be a math&nbsp;&nbsp; PhD before you could contribute&nbsp; to the frontier of math research.&nbsp; But now it's quite possible at the&nbsp; high school level, or whatever,&nbsp;&nbsp;

that you could get involved in a math project and&nbsp; actually make a real contribution because of all&nbsp;&nbsp; these AI tools, Lean, and everything else. There will be a lot of non-traditional&nbsp;&nbsp; opportunities to learn, so you&nbsp;

need a very adaptable mindset.&nbsp; There will be room for pursuing things&nbsp; just for curiosity and for playing around.&nbsp; You still need to get your credentials. For a while it will still be important to&nbsp;&nbsp;

go through traditional education and learn&nbsp; math and science the old-fashioned way.&nbsp; But you should also be open to very different ways&nbsp; of doing science, some of which don't exist yet.&nbsp; It's a scary time, but also very exciting.

That's a great note to close on. Terence,&nbsp;&nbsp; thanks so much. Pleasure.

> ## Key Points
> 
> - *Kepler’s Approach as Early Data Science:* Trial-and-error hypothesis testing grounded in Tycho Brahe’s precise observational data led to the first accurate model of planetary orbits (ellipses vs. circles) (00:00–00:04:22).  
> - *AI’s Role is Shifting Science Bottlenecks:* AI excels at generating vast numbers of hypotheses; the new bottleneck is systematic validation and assessment of scientific ideas at scale (00:04:22–00:13:21).  
> - *Scientific Progress Involves Culture and Narrative:* Beyond raw data and theories, social acceptance, communication, and storytelling drive the adoption of new scientific ideas (00:13:22–00:18:45).  
> - *Serendipity and Unstructured Exploration Are Crucial:* Accidental discoveries and random interactions foster creative leaps that highly optimized workflows risk losing (00:18:45–00:26:52, 01:07:53–01:16:06).  
> - *AI Triumphs in Breadth, Humans in Depth:* AI can quickly solve many simpler problems or identify partial paths, but humans provide deep insight, creativity, and interpretability (00:26:52–00:36:54).  
> - *Mathematical Research Values Process, Not Just Results:* The journey of discovery cultivates intuition and expertise; immediate answers from AI might risk hampering deep understanding (00:36:54–00:43:42).  
> - *Current AI Mostly Applies Known Techniques:* AI workflows often replicate and recombine existing methods better than humans but rarely create new theories (00:43:42–00:49:06).  
> - *Intelligence vs. Cleverness:* True intelligence requires cumulative learning and adapting strategies interactively, something current AIs cannot yet replicate (00:49:06–00:56:59).  
> - *Formal Languages and Proof Assistants Enable Precise Analysis:* Tools like Lean can decompose proofs into atomic units, facilitating AI collaboration in proof refinement and understanding (00:57:00–01:02:27).  
> - *Measuring Scientific Progress is Complex:* Progress depends on historical context, validation over time, and often retrospective acceptance, complicating how AI might assess scientific merit (01:02:27–01:07:53).  
> - *AI Will Reshape Scientific Workflows:* Future science will rely on broad AI-generated hypotheses and human expert interpretation, requiring new scientific and publication paradigms (01:16:06–01:23:11).  
> - *Advice for Aspiring Mathematicians:* Stay adaptable, leverage AI tools early, embrace new ways of doing science, and cultivate openness to both traditional and emerging methods (01:23:11–End).  
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Key Insights
> 
> - 🪐 *Analogy of Kepler as an Early “high-temperature LLM”* (00:04:00): Kepler’s process of trying random geometric hypotheses resembles how large language models explore solution spaces—intuitive but needing validation.  
> - 🧩 *Bottleneck Shift from Idea Generation to Validation* (00:12:00): AI exponentially lowers the cost of generating hypotheses, creating urgent demand for scalable validation frameworks, peer review, and filtering mechanisms.  
> - 📊 *AI and Data-First Hypothesis Generation* (00:08:00): Unlike traditional model-first science, modern science is increasingly data-driven—observations precede hypotheses. AI can amplify this data-first method.  
> - 🌄 *Mountain Climbing Metaphor for AI in Math* (00:32:00): AI can summit smaller, more accessible “walls” (problems) in math but struggles with deeper challenges due to lack of partial progress evaluation.  
> - 🚀 *Complementarity of AI Breadth and Human Depth* (00:35:00): Human experts have unparalleled depth in complex reasoning, while AI offers unparalleled breadth, enabling new modes of collaborative science.  
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
> 
> *Q1: Can AI independently solve major unsolved math problems like the Riemann hypothesis?*  
> *A:* Likely not fully autonomously. Such problems probably require new conceptual math beyond brute force and will involve deep human-AI collaboration and insight (00:53:00–00:56:59).
> 
> *Q2: How do we distinguish between useful AI-generated scientific ideas and noise?*  
> *A:* Current methods are overwhelmed. New validation, peer review, and possibly automated scientific frameworks are needed to filter progress reliably (00:12:00–00:14:00).
> 
> *Q3: Does AI improve mathematical productivity or mainly routine tasks?*  
> *A:* AI currently accelerates auxiliary and routine tasks, enriching outputs, but the core deep creative processes still rely on human insight for now (00:47:00–00:49:30).
> 
> *Q4: How important is serendipity in science and math discovery?*  
> *A:* Crucial—random encounters and inefficient exploration foster unexpected insights that systematic optimization often misses (01:07:53–01:16:06).
> 
> *Q5: How can early-career mathematicians prepare for an AI-influenced research landscape?*  
> *A:* Be adaptable, embrace AI tools, pursue both traditional credentials and innovative methods, and remain curious and open to different problem-solving approaches (01:21:00–End).
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Conclusion
> 
> The conversation with Terence Tao underscores that the nature of scientific progress is evolving alongside AI—not by replacing human creativity but by augmenting it, particularly by massively lowering the cost of exploration and hypothesis generation. Historical breakthroughs were forged through painstaking data collection paired with inspired hypothesis testing, a process AI now accelerates at unprecedented scales. Yet, the critical bottleneck remains rigorous validation, discernment, and the artful human narrative that cements scientific ideas into lasting knowledge. Future scientific success hinges on rethinking workflows to harness AI’s breadth with human depth, fostering new hybrid collaboration modes, and preserving the randomness and serendipity essential for innovation.
> 
> *Action Suggestions:*  
> - Develop scalable validation systems for handling AI-generated scientific outputs.  
> - Foster interdisciplinary collaboration combining AI expertise with deep human insight.  
> - Encourage early-career researchers to adopt flexible learning strategies incorporating AI tools.  
> - Promote new scientific communication paradigms that blend formal rigor with accessible narratives.  
> - Support research into semi-formal frameworks capturing scientific reasoning beyond formal proofs.
> 
> The video invites viewers to embrace the uncertain yet thrilling transformation of science by AI, where tradition meets innovation to redefine discovery’s future.

> ## Summary
> 
> This video presents an extensive and insightful conversation with Terence Tao, a preeminent mathematician, exploring the evolving landscape of scientific discovery, especially the role of AI in mathematics and research. The central theme is how historical scientific breakthroughs, like Kepler’s laws of planetary motion, emerged from a blend of hypothesis, data, and iteration—and how AI might transform this process today and in the future. The discussion emphasizes the complementary relationship between human creativity and AI’s brute force capabilities, the challenges in scientific validation with AI-generated ideas, and the importance of evolving scientific methods to harness AI’s strengths.
> 
> *Who is it suitable for:*  
> - Mathematicians, scientists, and researchers interested in AI’s impact on scientific discovery.  
> - Students and professionals curious about the history and philosophy of science.  
> - AI enthusiasts wanting to understand the challenges and opportunities in integrating AI with math research.  
> 
> *What readers can learn:*  
> - The history of scientific discovery framed through Kepler and Newton’s contributions.  
> - A detailed analysis of AI’s role in hypothesis generation versus validation in science.  
> - Insights into how mathematics and science workflows might shift with AI augmentation.  
> - The differences between clever problem-solving and genuine scientific intelligence.  
> - Practical advice for early-career mathematicians and scientists navigating an AI-augmented landscape.  
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Timeline Summary
> 
> *00:00–00:04:22 | Kepler’s Discovery and Early Scientific Data*  
> Terence recounts Kepler’s path from Copernicus’s heliocentric model to his Platonic solids theory and how Tycho Brahe’s precise data enabled the breakthrough discovery that planetary orbits are elliptical, laying the foundations of modern astronomy.
> 
> Conclusion: Early science balanced elegant hypothesis generation with meticulous data collection, highlighting the necessity of both.
> 
> ---
> 
> *00:04:22–00:07:38 | AI as a Modern Analogy to Historical Science*  
> Discussion about how Kepler’s trial-and-error method resembles modern AI’s random hypothesis generation, but with the essential twist that validation against high-quality data is crucial. The bottleneck has shifted from idea generation to systematic verification.
> 
> Conclusion: AI can generate ideas at scale, but scientific progress relies heavily on verifying and vetting these ideas.
> 
> ---
> 
> *00:07:38–00:13:21 | The Changing Paradigm of Scientific Discovery*  
> Science has evolved from theory-experiment to simulation and now big data-driven hypothesis generation. The increase in AI-generated scientific output creates an urgent need to redesign peer review and validation systems to handle the flood of ideas.
> 
> Conclusion: The scalability of idea generation demands new, scalable ways to evaluate scientific merit.
> 
> ---
> 
> *00:13:22–00:18:45 | Long-Term Validation and Scientific Culture*  
> Examples from history show that new theories often face initial resistance or are less accurate than existing ones yet provide deeper understanding long-term. The social narrative and communication of science play a critical role in acceptance and progress.
> 
> Conclusion: Scientific progress is iterative, sometimes contentious, and dependent on culture and communication.
> 
> ---
> 
> *00:18:45–00:26:52 | Serendipity, Insight, and the Deductive Overhang in Science*  
> Tao highlights the importance of serendipity, narrative-building, and deep insight in science, with examples from Darwin’s clear exposition to the patterns hidden in prime numbers. Astronomy particularly exemplifies squeezing maximal information from scarce data.
> 
> Conclusion: Both intuition and serendipitous discovery are essential complements to data and theory.
> 
> ---
> 
> *00:26:52–00:33:32 | AI-Assisted Problem Solving and the Erdős Problems*  
> The discussion covers AI’s mixed success solving Erdős math problems: initial rapid gains by solving “low-hanging fruit” were followed by a plateau. Tao uses a mountain-climbing analogy to describe AI jumping over easier barriers but struggling with deeper, complex hurdles.
> 
> Conclusion: AI excels at breadth and brute-force problem tackling but struggles with nuanced partial progress.
> 
> ---
> 
> *00:33:32–00:36:54 | Complementarity of Human Depth and AI Breadth in Science*  
> Terence and the host agree that AI’s strength is breadth, mapping broad fields and easy wins, while human experts focus on depth. Science workflows must adapt to this new model of wide-ranging AI exploration combined with focused human insight.
> 
> Conclusion: Future science will be a complementary collaboration, leveraging both AI’s and humans’ unique strengths.
> 
> ---
> 
> *00:36:54–00:43:42 | Differences Between Programming and Mathematical Research*  
> Discussion about how programming productivity increases with AI differ from math research, as the latter values the deep process of discovery, intuition building, and theory creation, not just results. AI can handle many routine tasks but cannot yet replace core mathematical creativity.
> 
> Conclusion: Core intellectual breakthroughs remain human-driven for now, though AI enriches auxiliary work.
> 
> ---
> 
> *00:43:42–00:49:06 | AI’s Current Limits and Incremental Gains in Mathematics*  
> Tao emphasizes that AI mostly excels by applying existing techniques and occasionally combining overlooked results rather than inventing fundamentally new math ideas. Success rates are low, but AI’s scale allows picking rare successes, while top math requires new conceptual breakthroughs.
> 
> Conclusion: AI is a powerful assistant for existing methods but not yet a source of revolutionary techniques.
> 
> ---
> 
> *00:49:06–00:56:59 | Intelligence vs. Cleverness and Interactive Problem Solving*  
> Intelligence involves cumulative, adaptive progress building upon partial solutions, which AI currently lacks. Present AI relies on trial and error without deep memory or evolving understanding. Tao envisions future mathematicians winnowing and refining AI-generated proofs to find elegance.
> 
> Conclusion: Genuine intelligence requires sustained cumulative reasoning—a frontier yet to be reached by AI.
> 
> ---
> 
> *00:57:00–01:02:27 | Formal Proofs, Narrative Science, and Semi-Formal Languages*  
> The power of formal proof assistants like Lean to break down proofs into atomic steps is discussed, along with the need for semi-formal languages that can integrate narrative and data-based scientific reasoning, enabling better AI-assisted conjecture generation and validation.
> 
> Conclusion: Bridging formal and natural scientific discourse is a key challenge to harnessing AI for science progress.
> 
> ---
> 
> *01:02:27–01:07:53 | The Nature of Conjectures and Scientific Progress Measurement*  
> Examples like the prime number theorem illustrate conjectures developed via data and intuition long before formal proofs. The difficulty of quantifying progress in such open-ended tasks is highlighted, as is the challenge of forecasting scientific success without multiple independent histories.
> 
> Conclusion: Understanding and measuring scientific progress requires novel frameworks and possibly simulated scientific environments.
> 
> ---
> 
> *01:07:53–01:16:06 | Serendipity, Scientific Interaction, and Modern Distractions*  
> Tao reflects on the value of random interactions and accidental discoveries, which are diminished in digitally optimized workflows. Distraction and unstructured time can foster breakthrough thinking, challenging how AI and modern work affect creativity and progress.
> 
> Conclusion: Preserving serendipity and unplanned interactions remains vital for creativity in a highly optimized world.
> 
> ---
> 
> *01:16:06–01:23:11 | The Future of AI and Mathematical Frontiers*  
> Thoughts on when AI might perform at or beyond Terence Tao's level suggest a near future where many traditional math tasks are AI-assisted or automated, but true frontier breakthroughs require hybrid human-AI collaboration. The evolution of mathematical practice and discovery methods will be profound.
> 
> Conclusion: AI will revolutionize math workflows but not supplant the need for human mathematical creativity anytime soon.
> 
> ---
> 
> *01:23:11–End | Advice for Early Career Mathematicians in an AI Age*  
> Tao advises embracing change and adaptability, leveraging new AI tools to contribute earlier than before, and remaining open to new scientific methods. Traditional education remains valuable but should be augmented by novel approaches to keep pace with evolving science landscapes.
> 
> Conclusion: Flexibility and openness to new paradigms will be key for success in math careers amid rapid technological change.
